meta.blurb: Ali Hafed sells his farm and sets out to find diamonds. Back home, the man who bought it leads his camel to the garden stream. Russell Conwell told this tale thousands of times, to ask where your own chances hide.
meta.bible: Russell H. Conwell: an American preacher, teacher and speaker who lived from the nineteenth into the twentieth century; he gave the lecture Acres of Diamonds thousands of times. He served in the Union army in the American Civil War, then worked as a lawyer and became a minister. Temple University: the school in Philadelphia that grew from his evening classes for working people. Ali Hafed: the Persian farmer in the tale, who lived near the Indus. Indus: the river near his farm. Persia: where the tale is set. Golconda: the famous diamond mine in the tale. Tigris and Euphrates: the rivers where Conwell said a guide told him the tale. Pennsylvania, California and Spain are places named in the book. Philadelphia is the city of Conwell's church and school. Voice and tone: warm, plain, practical and encouraging; the tales are told as tales ("the story says"); Conwell's opinions are given as his opinions; gentle modern notes where his views are disputed; no invented quotes, numbers or events. Full-length additions. Conwell: born 15 August 1843 on a hill farm in South Worthington, Massachusetts; he went to Yale, served as an officer in the Union army in the Civil War, studied law at Albany in New York, worked as a lawyer in Minneapolis and Boston, wrote for newspapers and travelled in Europe, the Middle East and Asia; he became a Baptist minister in Lexington, Massachusetts in 1879 and moved to Grace Baptist Church in Philadelphia in 1882; he died in 1925, aged eighty-two. Baptist Temple: the very large church in Philadelphia that opened in 1891. Temple College began in 1884 as evening classes for working people and became Temple University in 1907. Samaritan Hospital: the Philadelphia hospital Conwell helped to found for the sick, including those who could not pay. Baghdad and Babylon: places Conwell said he travelled to when a guide told him the tale. Mesopotamia: the land between the Tigris and Euphrates. Persia: the old name of Iran. Indus: the great river that rises in Tibet, flows through Pakistan and reaches the Arabian Sea. The tale: a priest tells Ali Hafed that the first diamond was a drop of sunlight turned to stone and that a river running over white sand between high mountains holds diamonds; Ali Hafed sells his farm, leaves his family with a neighbour, searches from the Mountains of the Moon to Palestine and Europe, and at last ends his life at a bay near Barcelona, in Spain. The man who buys his farm sees a flash in the white sand of the garden stream when his camel drinks, and the priest later knows the stone for a diamond. The garden proves rich in diamonds; the tale calls the mine Golconda. Golconda: the real fortress and diamond region is in India near Hyderabad. Koh-i-Noor: a famous old diamond now part of the British crown jewels. Kimberley: the South African diamond field with the Big Hole, dug almost all by hand. Pennsylvania oil: oil seeped from the ground long before Edwin Drake drilled the 1859 well near Titusville; the oil farm story is Conwell's. California gold: James Marshall found gold in January 1848 in the millrace of John Sutter's mill at Coloma; the rush that followed is called the forty-niners. Inventors named as true examples: Elisha Otis (the safety lift, shown at the New York Crystal Palace in 1854), Margaret Knight (flat-bottomed paper bags, patented 1871), Josephine Cochrane (dishwasher, patented 1886), Jacob Davis and Levi Strauss (riveted work trousers, patented 1873; Strauss opened a San Francisco dry-goods business in 1853). Benjamin Franklin learned printing from his older brother. Stephen Girard's school for poor boys opened in 1848; Peter Cooper founded Cooper Union in 1859; Franklin left money in his will for loans to young tradesmen in Philadelphia and Boston. Abraham Lincoln was born in 1809 in a log cabin in Kentucky. Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio, and made the first powered flights in December 1903 in North Carolina. Gilded Age: the American years of the 1870s to 1890s when some large fortunes were made unfairly. Bible: the letter of Timothy says the love of money is a root of evil. Conwell's opinions (that it is a duty to become rich honestly, that most rich people are honest, that most poor people are poor through their own fault) are given as his opinions, with modern notes that many things besides fault cause poverty.

What the Tale Is Really About

beats.scene: A tall man in a dark suit speaks to a packed hall
beats.summary: Russell Conwell stands before a full hall and gives his famous talk, Acres of Diamonds.

beats.scene: A calendar page, a hall door and a crowd of listeners spanning many years
beats.summary: He gave the same talk thousands of times over many years, by some counts more than six thousand.

beats.scene: A steam train crosses farmland while a man reads by the window
beats.summary: He travelled by train from town to town, so the talk reached farmers, clerks, teachers and shopkeepers.

beats.scene: A speaker's notes on a table, and a printed booklet beside them
beats.summary: The talk was spoken first and printed later, so a reader meets a speaker's voice on the page.

beats.scene: A wide green field marked into acres beside a football field
beats.summary: An acre is a measure of land, about the size of a football field, so acres of diamonds means treasure in plenty.

beats.scene: A rough diamond held up to the light between two fingers
beats.summary: Diamonds were the great symbol of wealth in Conwell's day, hard, rare and formed deep underground.

beats.scene: A paper plan with three boxes: a tale, a lesson, advice
beats.summary: The talk has a simple plan: a tale first, then what it means, then practical advice.

beats.scene: A farmer stands in his own field, looking down at the soil
beats.summary: Its main idea is that your best chance may lie close to home, where you already stand.

beats.scene: Ordinary people in work clothes sit close together in rows
beats.summary: It spoke to ordinary people who wanted a better life but did not know where to begin.

beats.scene: A door with light shining under it and a speaker's name on a plaque
beats.summary: Before the tale, it helps to know the man who told it.

beats.scene: A hill farm with stone walls and a farmhouse in autumn
beats.summary: Russell Conwell was born in 1843 on a farm in the hills of South Worthington, Massachusetts.

beats.scene: A farm boy walks to school with a book under his arm
beats.summary: He left the farm to study, and he went on to Yale.

beats.scene: A young soldier in a blue coat stands in a camp at dawn
beats.summary: When the American Civil War began, he joined the Union army and became an officer.

beats.scene: A young man in a law school classroom bends over a thick book
beats.summary: After the war he studied law, and he finished at the law school in Albany, New York.

beats.scene: A lawyer's desk in a small office with files and a lamp
beats.summary: He worked as a lawyer in Minneapolis and then in Boston.

beats.scene: A man writes in a notebook on a ship's deck near a far coast
beats.summary: He also wrote for newspapers and travelled in Europe, the Middle East and Asia.

beats.scene: A man in a plain church pulpit with a small congregation
beats.summary: In 1879 he became a Baptist minister in Lexington, Massachusetts.

beats.scene: A small brick church with a crowd waiting outside its doors
beats.summary: In 1882 he moved to a small church in Philadelphia, and it quickly grew crowded.

beats.scene: A huge new church with tall doors opens in a busy city street
beats.summary: A very large new church, the Baptist Temple, was built for the growing crowds.

beats.scene: A writer at a desk with a stack of finished books
beats.summary: Conwell also wrote many books, including life stories of well-known leaders.

beats.scene: A young man with a work cap knocks at the door of a study
beats.summary: In 1884 a young man asked Conwell to teach him, so that he could become a minister.

beats.scene: A lamp-lit room where a few working men sit with notebooks
beats.summary: Conwell taught him in the evenings, and soon other working people joined.

beats.scene: Church-hall classroom filled with evening students in work clothes
beats.summary: The evening classes grew, and the school was named Temple College.

beats.scene: A bundle of banknotes handed across a table to a school clerk
beats.summary: Much of the money Conwell earned from speaking went to the school.

beats.scene: A shopgirl and a clerk walk toward a lit school window after work
beats.summary: Students could work by day and study by night, so no one had to choose.

beats.scene: A nurse in a long apron beside a hospital bed
beats.summary: Conwell also helped to found a hospital in Philadelphia for people who could not pay.

beats.scene: A long row of graduates in caps and gowns on a wide lawn
beats.summary: In time the college became Temple University, with thousands of students.

beats.scene: A bearded man in a plain office signs a paper beside letters
beats.summary: Conwell led the school for the rest of his life.

beats.scene: A single small room and lamp, with a bigger building sketched behind
beats.summary: The school shows his own idea at work: see a need, start small and use what you have.

beats.scene: A bookmark placed in a book, a cover with a drawing of a river
beats.summary: Now comes the story that made the talk famous.

beats.scene: A wide brown river flows between dry banks under a hot sky
beats.summary: As a young man Conwell travelled in the Middle East, by the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.

beats.scene: A traveller and a guide walk beside a camel train past old ruins
beats.summary: He hired a guide to show him ancient cities such as Baghdad and Babylon.

beats.scene: A line of camels moves slowly across a dusty plain at midday
beats.summary: They travelled slowly across dry land, and the long days left plenty of time for stories.

beats.scene: An old guide with a wrapped headcloth gestures as he talks
beats.summary: The guide loved to talk, and he seemed to know a tale for every bend of the river.

beats.scene: Two men and their camels pause beside a quiet river
beats.summary: One day the guide offered to tell a tale about a Persian farmer who lived by the Indus.

beats.scene: A rolled old scroll tied with string on a low table
beats.summary: Nobody can say whether the tale is an old legend or a clever invention.

beats.scene: A map showing Persia, the Indus river and the sea beyond
beats.summary: Persia is the old name of the land now called Iran; the Indus is a great river farther east.

beats.scene: A man in a long coat stands on a farm porch, facing the sunrise
beats.summary: The guide called the farmer Ali Hafed, and in the tale he lived near the river Indus.

beats.scene: A traveller writing in a notebook by lamp light under a canvas roof
beats.summary: Conwell kept the tale and told it, in his own way, to crowds across America.

beats.scene: Two men sit by a fire at dusk; the guide raises one finger
beats.summary: Let us listen to the guide: a tale of a man who had everything and did not know it.

beats.scene: A wide farm beside a river, with fields, trees and a white house
beats.summary: Ali Hafed lived near the Indus on a large farm, and he was content.

beats.scene: Golden fields of grain wave in the wind under a clear sky
beats.summary: His fields of grain grew tall, and the harvests filled his barns.

beats.scene: Orchard trees heavy with ripe fruit and a ladder against a trunk
beats.summary: His orchards gave more fruit than his family could eat.

beats.scene: A small garden stream runs over pale sand between flower beds
beats.summary: A small stream ran through his garden over clean, pale sand.

beats.scene: A leather purse and a stack of coins on a wooden table
beats.summary: He had money put away and lent out at interest.

beats.scene: Children play by the garden stream while their mother calls them
beats.summary: He had a wife and children whom he loved dearly.

beats.scene: A farmer wakes at dawn and walks through his fields
beats.summary: His days followed the seasons: plough, plant, water and harvest.

beats.scene: A family eats supper by lamplight at a long wooden table
beats.summary: In the evenings the family ate together, and Ali Hafed felt himself a lucky man.

beats.scene: A scale balancing a small bag of coins against a happy family
beats.summary: Conwell's tale says he was contented because he was wealthy, and wealthy because he was contented.

beats.scene: A visitor's silhouette arrives at the farm gate at sunset
beats.summary: Then one evening a visitor arrived, and everything began to change.

beats.scene: An old priest in a plain robe sits by a fireside
beats.summary: The visitor was an old priest, a wise and learned man.

beats.scene: Fire light flickers on the wall as the priest speaks to the farmer
beats.summary: One cool evening the priest sat by the fire and told Ali Hafed how the world was made.

beats.scene: A glowing drop of sunlight hardens into a clear stone
beats.summary: The priest said the first diamond was a drop of sunlight that had turned to stone.

beats.scene: Layers of earth under a mountain with a glowing stone deep below
beats.summary: Today we know that diamonds are carbon, made far underground under great heat and pressure.

beats.scene: The priest holds up his thumb to show the size of a stone
beats.summary: He said a diamond as big as a thumb would buy many farms.

beats.scene: A pile of diamonds in two cupped hands
beats.summary: A handful of diamonds, he said, could buy a whole country.

beats.scene: Two boys in golden crowns sit on carved thrones
beats.summary: A mine of diamonds could set Ali Hafed's sons on thrones.

beats.scene: A man lies awake in the dark, looking at the ceiling
beats.summary: That night Ali Hafed went to bed poor, not because he had lost anything but because he wanted more.

beats.scene: A man sits up in bed at midnight, his face full of thoughts
beats.summary: He could not sleep, and he thought about diamonds until the sky grew pale.

beats.scene: A farmer shakes an old priest awake in the early dawn
beats.summary: At dawn he woke the priest and asked him where diamonds could be found.

beats.scene: A tired priest rubs his eyes and frowns at the farmer
beats.summary: The tired priest asked why Ali Hafed wanted diamonds so badly.

beats.scene: A river runs over white sand between two tall mountains
beats.summary: He told him to find a river that runs over white sand between high mountains.

beats.scene: The farmer kneels beside the priest, nodding with a bright face
beats.summary: Ali Hafed believed him, and he was filled with hope.

beats.scene: A farmer counts money into a bag while a buyer reads a paper
beats.summary: He sold his farm and gathered all the money that was owed to him.

beats.scene: A farmer's family stands with a neighbour at a garden gate
beats.summary: He left his wife and children in the care of a neighbour.

beats.scene: A lone man with a pack on his back walks down a long road
beats.summary: Then he set off alone to look for the river of white sand.

beats.scene: An old map of Africa, a mountain range marked Mountains of the Moon
beats.summary: His search began, in the tale, at the Mountains of the Moon, a range of legend at the source of the Nile.

beats.scene: A traveller on a hill looks over a harbour and old stone walls
beats.summary: From there he wandered on to Palestine and then through Europe.

beats.scene: A traveller stops at a river bank and kneels to look at its sand
beats.summary: At every river he stopped, looked at the sand and asked if it was white enough.

beats.scene: A calendar with torn pages and a thinning purse on a table
beats.summary: Months went by, then years, and the money in his purse grew less and less.

beats.scene: A man digs and sifts river sand in a pan
beats.summary: He sifted many riverbeds, but none held the diamonds the priest had described.

beats.scene: A tired traveller sleeps under open sky beside a dead fire
beats.summary: He slept in the open, crossed strange lands and could not speak the languages around him.

beats.scene: An empty purse turned upside down on the ground
beats.summary: At last his money was all gone.

beats.scene: A thin man in tattered clothes sits by a roadside with an empty bag
beats.summary: He became thin and hungry, dressed in rags.

beats.scene: A man gazes into the distance, remembering a farm and garden
beats.summary: He often thought of his farm, his garden and the children who played by the stream.

beats.scene: A man looks back along a long dusty road toward the horizon
beats.summary: He had promised himself to return a rich man, and he could not go home with nothing.

beats.scene: A bay with tall cliffs and a harbour full of ships
beats.summary: In the end his road led him to a bay near Barcelona, in Spain.

beats.scene: A ragged man stands alone on a shore as a huge wave rolls in
beats.summary: He stood on the shore, worn out, as a great wave rolled in from the sea.

beats.scene: A rough sea under a grey sky, with no one on the shore
beats.summary: In despair he threw himself into the tide, and he never came out alive.

beats.scene: An empty road leading to the horizon, with one bundle left on it
beats.summary: So ended the search of Ali Hafed, far from the home where his riches lay.

beats.scene: The same farm in morning light, with a stranger at the gate
beats.summary: Meanwhile the man who bought the farm had settled in, and he cared for it well.

beats.scene: A man leads a camel through the farm garden toward a stream
beats.summary: One day he led his camel to the garden stream to drink.

beats.scene: A camel dips its nose into shallow water over white sand
beats.summary: The camel put its nose into the shallow water.

beats.scene: A bright flash of light glints up from the sand under the water
beats.summary: As it lifted its head, the man saw a flash of light in the sand.

beats.scene: A man's wet hand holds a dark stone with a glowing spot
beats.summary: He picked out a dark stone with a spot of light inside it that showed every colour of the rainbow.

beats.scene: A stone is placed on a mantel above a fireplace beside a clock
beats.summary: He took it home, put it on the shelf above the fireplace and forgot about it.

beats.scene: The old priest walks up the farm path with his stick
beats.summary: A few days later the old priest came to visit the new owner.

beats.scene: The priest points at the glittering stone on the shelf
beats.summary: The priest saw the flash of light and cried out, "Here is a diamond!"

beats.scene: The priest asks and the farmer shrugs, holding out the stone
beats.summary: "Has Ali Hafed come home?" he asked, and the farmer said no, and that it was only a stone from the garden.

beats.scene: The priest tugs the farmer's sleeve toward the garden door
beats.summary: "I know a diamond when I see one," said the priest, and they ran to the garden.

beats.scene: Two men on their knees stirring white sand with their fingers
beats.summary: Together they stirred the white sand with their fingers.

beats.scene: Sparkling stones lie in the stirred sand, one bigger than the last
beats.summary: They found more stones, each more beautiful and more valuable than the first.

beats.scene: A grand gleaming mine entrance with sacks of gems
beats.summary: So the guide said, the great diamond mine of Golconda was found.

beats.scene: A fortress on a rocky hill over a plain, with towers
beats.summary: The real Golconda is in India, and the tale only borrows its famous name.

beats.scene: A crown in a glass case, lit from above, with a large central stone
beats.summary: Famous old diamonds, such as the Koh-i-Noor in the British crown jewels, came from that region of India.

beats.scene: A huge open pit in the ground with thousands of tiny workers
beats.summary: The guide said this mine beat even Kimberley, a diamond field in South Africa.

beats.scene: A child on a river bank holds up a pretty pebble to a neighbour
beats.summary: The usual story says a child found a pebble that proved to be a diamond on a South African farm in 1866.

beats.scene: Ali Hafed's old garden with a spade left stuck in the sand
beats.summary: The guide's lesson: had Ali Hafed stayed home and dug in his garden, he would have had acres of diamonds.

beats.scene: Rich jewels in rows lit by sun through a high window
beats.summary: In the tale, every shovelful of that old farm held jewels that later shone in the crowns of kings.

beats.scene: Split scene: a lonely tent far away, a glowing garden at home
beats.summary: Ali Hafed starved in a strange land while the treasure lay in the stream where his children played.

beats.scene: Two travellers rest after the story; one is thoughtful
beats.summary: Conwell said that the tale stayed with him long after the journey.

beats.scene: A man alone in a bedroom looks out a window at a field
beats.summary: Ali Hafed's real trouble was not poverty but discontent; the priest's words made him feel poor.

beats.scene: A scale with a wish on one side and a field on the other
beats.summary: Wanting to grow is not wrong; Conwell's point is to look at what you have first.

beats.scene: A man looks over a fence at a faraway hill that glows
beats.summary: The trap is the idea that the good chance is always somewhere else.

beats.scene: A person stands knee-deep in a stream and never looks down
beats.summary: Ali Hafed never asked what his own land held, and nobody asked it for him.

beats.scene: A crowd in a hall; the speaker points straight at them
beats.summary: Conwell told his listeners that they were standing in the middle of their own acres of diamonds.

beats.scene: A paper with words: skills, friends, needs, ideas, work
beats.summary: The diamonds stand for chances: skills, ideas, friends, work and the needs of the neighbours around you.

beats.scene: Hands stirring sand with effort, sweat on a forehead
beats.summary: Even in the tale, the diamonds had to be found by digging in the sand.

beats.scene: A road sign with two arrows; the man is thinking
beats.summary: Sometimes moving away is the right choice, and the tale does not claim otherwise.

beats.scene: A magnifying glass held over a city street
beats.summary: The useful question is whether you have really looked carefully where you are.

beats.scene: A farmer stands beside a creek with a dark, shiny film on its surface
beats.summary: Conwell next tells of a Pennsylvania farm, and its tale began in oil.

beats.scene: Old settlers skim dark oil from a creek with a blanket
beats.summary: People in western Pennsylvania had long seen oil seep from the ground and skimmed it from creeks.

beats.scene: A wooden derrick stands above a well in a green valley
beats.summary: In 1859 Edwin Drake drilled a well near Titusville, and oil flowed from about seventy feet down.

beats.scene: Farmers in work clothes sell their fields while wells rise behind them
beats.summary: In Conwell's telling, a farmer sold his farm and went far away to hunt for oil.

beats.scene: A man pushes a plank across a farm stream to block the dark film
beats.summary: The new owner kept a board in the stream to hold back the oily scum so his cattle could drink.

beats.scene: A well tower and storage tank stand where the old farm was
beats.summary: In the story, that farm lay above one of the richest oil fields in the region.

beats.scene: A young carpenter peers into a mill stream and finds yellow flakes
beats.summary: In January 1848 a carpenter named James Marshall found gold in the millrace at Sutter's Mill, in California.

beats.scene: Wagons and ships crowd the road and harbour, full of hopeful people
beats.summary: The news raced around the world, and by about 1855 some three hundred thousand people had come to California.

beats.scene: A prospector washes gravel in a pan, finding almost nothing
beats.summary: Few of them grew rich by digging, and many went home with little.

beats.scene: A shopkeeper counts coins at a busy tent store in the gold fields
beats.summary: Shopkeepers who sold tools, food and cloth often did better than the diggers, and the first finder was already at work on the spot.

beats.scene: A man stands at his own front door and looks along the street
beats.summary: Conwell's first rule is not to wait for a better time or place.

beats.scene: A neighbour talks across a garden fence, with a question mark floating above
beats.summary: He asked his listeners what the people around them lacked.

beats.scene: A speaker studies a town map and shop list in a hotel room
beats.summary: It is said that before each talk he learned about the town, so he could name chances in its own streets.

beats.scene: A mill, a school and a railway station along one main street
beats.summary: Picture a town with a school, a mill and a station: each has needs a person could meet.

beats.scene: A man packs a bag and looks uneasy at his own shadow
beats.summary: Moving away rarely cures worry, for the same person goes along.

beats.scene: A local shopkeeper greets customers by name
beats.summary: You know your town, your neighbours and your customs, and a stranger does not.

beats.scene: A friendly handshake across a counter
beats.summary: Neighbours know your name and your character, and trust makes customers come back.

beats.scene: A pile of moving boxes beside a bill and a new key
beats.summary: Starting over in a new place costs money, and trust has to be earned again from zero.

beats.scene: A man holds a spade at his own door, ready to start
beats.summary: Conwell did not mean sit still; he meant begin today, with what is in front of you.

beats.scene: A notebook with five written needs of a street
beats.summary: Try it: write five things people in your street lack or complain about, and each is a possible start.

beats.scene: A shopkeeper listens to a customer and takes notes
beats.summary: Conwell's rule for finding the diamond is to find out what people need, and then supply it.

beats.scene: A coin passes from a woman's hand to a baker's hand for bread
beats.summary: People pay for what helps them, not for what the maker happens to like.

beats.scene: A man rides a lift platform high above a crowded hall
beats.summary: In 1854 Elisha Otis showed a safety brake for lifts at the New York Crystal Palace; it made tall buildings safer to use.

beats.scene: A woman sketches a flat-bottomed paper bag beside a machine
beats.summary: Margaret Knight worked in a paper-bag factory and invented a machine for flat-bottomed bags, patented in 1871.

beats.scene: A woman in a long dress stands beside a wooden dish-washing machine
beats.summary: Josephine Cochrane wanted to protect her good dishes, and in 1886 she patented a dishwasher.

beats.scene: A tailor rivets a pocket on a pair of work trousers
beats.summary: A tailor named Jacob Davis put rivets in work trousers, and with Levi Strauss he gained a patent in 1873.

beats.scene: A sewing needle, a pocket and a worried face
beats.summary: Each began with a real, small problem that someone else had noticed and fixed.

beats.scene: Three question signs: What is hard? What takes long? What is paid for?
beats.summary: Ask what people near you find hard, what wastes their time, and what they already pay others to do.

beats.scene: A tailor, a cook and a teacher at work in a busy village
beats.summary: Not everyone invents a machine; teaching, cooking, mending and caring also meet needs.

beats.scene: A neighbour hands over a bag of tools to a friend
beats.summary: Learning what people need takes attention: watch, ask and listen.

beats.scene: A small shop with a handwritten sign and a few shelves
beats.summary: Conwell says to start small, where you are and with what you have.

beats.scene: A man shows an idea to a customer rather than money
beats.summary: A good start needs attention more than cash.

beats.scene: A kitchen table covered with sewing, sales slips and a lamp
beats.summary: Many firms began in a kitchen, a shed or a corner of a shop.

beats.scene: A modest stack of goods and a small coin tray on a bench
beats.summary: A small start lets you learn cheaply, since early mistakes cost little.

beats.scene: A neighbour tells another over a fence about a good seller
beats.summary: Your first customers are neighbours, and they tell others.

beats.scene: A jar on a shelf slowly filling with coins
beats.summary: Put aside a little each week; a small saving is a seed.

beats.scene: A tall store with a shop window, with a tiny shop sketched beside it
beats.summary: Levi Strauss began as a dry-goods merchant in San Francisco in 1853; great firms often begin small.

beats.scene: Two brothers build a wooden-winged flying machine in a bicycle workshop
beats.summary: Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton and built the first powered aeroplane with its tools and skills.

beats.scene: A staircase with the first step lit
beats.summary: When one step works, take the next; do not try to leap to the top.

beats.scene: A paper with three steps: need, plan, begin
beats.summary: The advice in three steps is to find a real need, plan a way to meet it, and begin.

beats.scene: A person holds a glowing stone beside a hammer, a pen and a book
beats.summary: Your own skills, friends and surroundings are your acres of diamonds.

beats.scene: A craftsman practises at a bench, a book open beside him
beats.summary: Learning and practising a skill makes you more useful, and a useful person is always in demand.

beats.scene: A crowd of evening students at a school door
beats.summary: This is why Conwell started evening classes: learning was a way of digging.

beats.scene: A boy in a print shop sets type beside his older brother
beats.summary: Benjamin Franklin learned the printing trade as a boy, working for his older brother.

beats.scene: A worker repeats a task slowly, with a calendar showing many days
beats.summary: A skill is built by steady practice, a little each day.

beats.scene: A farmer in shirt sleeves digs a field, sweat on his face
beats.summary: A farmer knows there is no shortcut to a good harvest; the richest ground still has to be dug.

beats.scene: A traveller in a green field gazes at a greener field far away
beats.summary: Distant fields look greener; Ali Hafed's story warns against envy of faraway things.

beats.scene: A boy asks an older woman questions at her doorstep
beats.summary: Begin by serving the people nearest to you: family, neighbours and townspeople.

beats.scene: A circle of friends around a table, sharing a meal and talking
beats.summary: Friends and neighbours are part of the treasure, so do not neglect them in your search.

A1A2: Russell Conwell stands before a big crowd and starts his famous talk.
Conwell gave this same talk thousands of times, in many different towns.
He travelled by train to reach people in towns and villages.
The talk was spoken first and printed in a book later.
An acre is a piece of land about as big as a football field.
Diamonds are hard, rare and costly, so people see them as treasure.
The talk has a plan: first a tale, then a lesson, then advice.
His main idea is that your best chance may be close to home.
The talk was for ordinary people who wanted a better life.
Before we hear the tale, let us meet the man who told it.
Conwell was born in 1843 on a farm in the hills.
He left the farm to study, and later he went to Yale.
When the Civil War began, he left college to join the army.
After the war he studied law in the city of Albany.
He worked as a lawyer, first in Minneapolis and then in Boston.
He also wrote for newspapers and travelled to far countries.
In 1879 he became a church minister in a small town.
In 1882 he moved to a small church in Philadelphia.
A very large new church, the Baptist Temple, was built for the crowds.
Conwell also wrote many books during his long and busy life.
In 1884 a young man asked Conwell to teach him at night.
Soon other working men and women came to learn too.
The classes grew, and the school was named Temple College.
Much of the money he earned from speaking went to the school.
Students could work by day and study at night.
Conwell also helped start a hospital for people who could not pay.
In time the school became Temple University, with thousands of students.
Conwell led the school for the rest of his long life.
The school shows his idea at work: see a need, start small.
Now comes the story that made the talk so famous.
As a young man Conwell travelled beside two great rivers.
In Baghdad he hired a guide to show him old ruins.
They moved slowly across the dry land, and the days were long.
The guide loved to talk, and he knew many tales.
One day the guide offered to tell him a special story.
Nobody can say if the tale is very old or quite new.
Persia is the old name for the country now called Iran.
In the guide's tale the farmer was a man named Ali Hafed.
Conwell never forgot the tale, and later he told it to crowds.
Let us listen to the tale of a man who had everything.
Ali Hafed lived near the Indus on a large farm.
His fields of grain grew tall in the summer sun.
His orchards gave more fruit than his family could eat.
A small stream ran through his garden over clean, pale sand.
He also had money put away, and it earned him interest.
He had a wife and children whom he loved dearly.
His days followed the seasons: dig, plant, water and harvest.
In the evenings the family ate together, and Ali Hafed was happy.
He was content because he was rich, and rich because content.
Then one evening a visitor came, and everything began to change.
The visitor was an old priest, wise and kind.
One cool evening the priest sat by the fire and spoke.
The priest said the first diamond was a drop of sunlight.
Today we know that diamonds are made of carbon.
He said a diamond as big as a thumb would buy many farms.
A handful of diamonds, the priest said, could buy a whole country.
With a whole mine, Ali Hafed could put his sons on thrones.
That night Ali Hafed felt poor, though he had lost nothing.
He could not sleep, and he thought about diamonds all night.
At dawn he woke the priest and asked where diamonds were.
The tired priest asked why he wanted diamonds so badly.
The priest told him to find a river with white sand.
Ali Hafed believed every word, and his heart was full of hope.
He sold his farm and collected all the money he was owed.
He left his wife and children with a good neighbour.
Then he set off alone to look for the river of white sand.
In the tale, his search began at the Mountains of the Moon.
From there he walked on to Palestine and then to Europe.
At every river he stopped and looked closely at the sand.
Months and years passed, and his purse grew lighter and lighter.
He looked in many rivers, but he found no diamonds.
He slept outside and crossed many lands where he knew no one.
At last the money was all gone, and he had nothing left.
He became thin and hungry, and his clothes were rags.
He often thought about his farm and the garden stream.
He could not go home with empty hands, so he walked on.
At last his road led him to the sea, in Spain.
He stood on the shore, tired, as a great wave came.
In despair he gave himself to the tide and was lost.
So ended the search of Ali Hafed, far from the home he left.
Back at the farm, the new owner took good care of the land.
One day the new owner led his camel to the garden stream.
The camel put its nose into the shallow water.
As it lifted its head, he saw a flash in the sand.
He picked up a dark stone with a bright spot of light.
He took it home, put it on a shelf and forgot it.
A few days later the old priest came to visit him.
The priest saw the shining stone and shouted that it was a diamond.
He asked if Ali Hafed had come home, and the answer was no.
“I know a diamond when I see one,” said the priest.
Together they stirred the white sand with their fingers.
They found more stones, each more beautiful than the first.
According to the guide, this is how Golconda was found.
The real Golconda is in India, and the tale only borrows its name.
Some very famous diamonds came from that part of the world.
Kimberley, in South Africa, was another great diamond field.
In 1866 a boy found a pretty stone, and it was a diamond.
The guide said Ali Hafed should have stayed home and dug.
Every spade of earth on that old farm held jewels fit for kings.
Ali Hafed went hungry and cold in a strange land far away.
Conwell said the tale stayed with him long after the trip.
Ali Hafed's real trouble was not poverty but discontent.
Wanting a better life is good, but look at what you have first.
The trap is to think that good chances are always far away.
Ali Hafed never asked what treasures his own land held.
Conwell told his listeners they were standing in acres of diamonds.
The diamonds stand for chances: skills, ideas, friends and work.
Even in the tale, the diamonds had to be found by stirring the sand.
Sometimes moving away is the right choice for a person.
The useful question is whether you have really looked around you.
Conwell next tells of a farm in Pennsylvania, far from Persia.
In western Pennsylvania, oil sometimes came up out of the ground.
In 1859 Edwin Drake drilled a well near Titusville.
In the story, a farmer sold his farm to look for oil.
The new owner saw a dark film on the stream.
Under that farm lay one of the richest oil fields around.
In 1848 a carpenter found gold in a mill stream in California.
News of the gold spread, and thousands rushed to California.
Few people grew rich by digging, and many went home poor.
Shopkeepers who sold tools and food often did better than miners.
Conwell says do not wait for a better time or place.
He asked listeners what the people around them lacked.
It is said he studied each town before he spoke there.
A town with a station needs people to carry goods.
Moving away does not cure worry, for you take yourself along.
You know your town and your neighbours, and a stranger does not.
Your neighbours know you, and they will trust you more.
Starting again in a new place costs money and time.
Conwell did not mean sit still; he meant start today.
Try it: write down five things your neighbours lack.
To find the diamond, find what people need and supply it.
People pay for what helps them, not for what you like.
In 1854 Elisha Otis showed a safety brake for lifts.
Margaret Knight invented a machine that made flat paper bags.
Josephine Cochrane built a machine to wash dishes in 1886.
A tailor put metal studs in work trousers, and they sold well.
Each of them began with one small, real problem.
Ask what is hard, what takes too long, and what people pay for.
Not everyone invents a machine; many people simply serve others.
Learning what people need takes patience and careful attention.
Conwell says to start small, where you are, with what you have.
A good start needs more attention than money.
Many firms began in a kitchen, a shed or a shop corner.
A small start lets you learn, and mistakes cost little.
Your first customers are neighbours, and they tell others.
Put aside a little each week, and it will grow.
Levi Strauss began with a small shop that sold cloth and clothes.
The Wright brothers began in a small bicycle shop.
When one small step works, you can take the next one.
The advice in three steps: find a need, plan, and begin.
Your own skills and friends are your acres of diamonds.
Learning a skill makes you more useful to other people.
Conwell started evening classes so that working people could learn.
Benjamin Franklin learned the printing trade as a boy.
A skill is built by steady practice, a little each day.
A farmer knows there is no shortcut to a good harvest.
Distant fields look greener, but they may not be.
Begin by serving the people nearest to you.
Friends and neighbours are part of the treasure too.
A useful person always has work to do.
Conwell said it is right to get rich in an honest way.
Many good people think that wanting money is wrong.
The Bible warns against the love of money, not money itself.
An honest seller who serves customers well earns their trust.
Not every fortune in Conwell's time was earned honestly.
A good name takes many years to build, but is lost fast.
Conwell held that most poor people were poor through their own fault.
Many people today see more causes of poverty than that.
Still, he believed in helping people who work to improve.
Honest effort is good, but do not judge the poor too fast.

Stephen Girard left money for a school for poor boys.
Peter Cooper started a college for working people in New York.
Benjamin Franklin left money to lend to young craftsmen.
Conwell asked the rich to give wisely, not just to keep.
You do not need to be rich to give something.

Wealth is also health, family, friends and good work.
Ali Hafed had all of these, and left them for a dream.

A teacher in a small school can change many lives.
Abraham Lincoln was born in a log cabin in Kentucky.
Conwell himself was a boy from a hill farm.
Many great people come from small towns and plain homes.
Every famous person was once an unknown neighbour.
You can be great in small things, like a kept promise.
A person who serves others in town becomes known and trusted.
Fame soon fades, but a useful life is long remembered.
Greatness is open to everyone, and it can start today.

Where barriers are real, people can work together to change them.

B1B2: A tall man in a dark suit walks onto a stage in front of a full hall. His name is Russell Conwell, and he is about to give the talk that made him famous.
Conwell gave the talk again and again for many years. By most counts he gave it thousands of times, and some people say more than six thousand.
Conwell travelled by train from town to town, carrying his talk with him. In this way it reached farmers, clerks, teachers and shopkeepers who would never have visited a big city.
Acres of Diamonds began as a spoken lecture, not as a written book. It was printed later, so when you read it you are hearing a speaker's voice.
An acre is a measure of land, about as big as a football field. So acres of diamonds means a treasure so large that it covers the ground.
In Conwell's day a diamond was the great symbol of wealth. It is the hardest natural material, it is rare, and it forms deep under the ground.
The talk follows a very simple plan, in three parts. It begins with a tale, then explains what the tale means, and finishes with practical advice.
His main idea is easy to say, though hard to live by. Your best chance in life may lie close to home, where you already stand.
The talk was meant for ordinary people who wanted a better life but did not know where to begin. It offered them a new way of looking at their own town.
Before we hear the tale, it helps to know the man who told it. His own life, like a good story, had many surprising turns.
Russell Conwell was born in 1843 on a hill farm in western Massachusetts. The nearest village was South Worthington, a small place among the hills.
As a boy Conwell wanted to learn more than the farm could teach him. He went away to school, and then he entered Yale College.
When the American Civil War began, Conwell left his studies and joined the Union army. He rose to become an officer and led a company of soldiers.
After the war ended, Conwell turned to the law. He studied at a law school in Albany, New York, and finished his course there.
He began work as a lawyer in Minneapolis, which was then a young city in the Midwest. Later he returned to the east and practised law in Boston.
Conwell also worked as a writer for several newspapers of his time. His work took him to Europe, the Middle East and Asia, where he saw how other people lived.
In 1879 Conwell became a Baptist minister after years of other work. His first church was in Lexington, Massachusetts, a small town near Boston.
In 1882 Conwell moved to a small church in Philadelphia. It was called Grace Baptist Church, and it soon grew crowded.
To hold the crowds, a very large new church was built in Philadelphia. It was called the Baptist Temple, and it opened in 1891.
Besides preaching and teaching, Conwell found time to write many books. Among them were life stories of well-known leaders of his time.
One evening in 1884 a young man came to Conwell with a request. He wanted to become a minister, and he asked Conwell to teach him.
Conwell taught him in the evenings, and soon others asked to join. They were young people who worked all day and could only study at night.
The evening classes grew larger each year, and the school was given a name. It was called Temple College, after the church where it began.
Conwell gave much of the money he earned from his lectures to the school. In this way the talk about diamonds helped to pay for something real.
Students could work all day and study in the evening, so no one had to choose between earning a living and learning. For many of them this opened a door that would otherwise have stayed shut.
Conwell also helped to start a hospital in Philadelphia, called the Samaritan Hospital. It was founded to care for sick people, including those who could not pay.
In 1907 the college became Temple University, with the right to give degrees. Over the years it grew to teach many thousands of students.
Conwell led the school for the rest of his long life. He died in 1925, in Philadelphia, at the age of eighty-two.
The school shows his own advice being put to work. He saw a need, he started small, and he used what he already had.
Now it is time for the story that made the talk famous. It begins far from Philadelphia, beside a great river in the Middle East.
As a young man, Conwell travelled through the lands of the Middle East. His journey took him along the Tigris and Euphrates, two great rivers in what is now Iraq.
At Baghdad, Conwell hired a guide to take him to the ruins of ancient cities such as Babylon. The guide knew the roads, the ruins and the old stories of the land.
They travelled slowly across dry, dusty land, with camels carrying the baggage. The days were long, and there was plenty of time for stories.
The guide was a man who loved to talk about the places they passed. He seemed to know a tale for every bend of the river.
One day the guide offered to tell Conwell a very special tale. It was about a Persian farmer who lived beside the river Indus.
Nobody can say whether the tale is an ancient legend or a clever invention. Folk tales travel by word of mouth, and each storyteller adds a little.
Persia is the old name of the country that is now called Iran. The Indus is a great river that begins in the mountains of Tibet and flows through Pakistan to the sea.
In the guide's tale, the farmer was a man named Ali Hafed. He lived on the banks of the Indus, a long way from the place where Conwell listened.
Conwell never forgot the guide's tale, and he kept it in his memory for years. Later he told it in his own words to crowds all over America.
So let us pause beside the river at dusk and listen to the guide. It is a tale about a man who had everything and did not know it.
Ali Hafed lived on a large farm beside the river Indus. He had everything a farmer could want, and he was content.
Ali Hafed's fields of grain grew tall in the sun. Every harvest filled his barns, and there was always some left over.
His orchards were full of trees that gave fruit every year. In the season there was more than his family could eat.
Near the house was a garden, and a small stream flowed through it. The water ran clear and shallow over clean, pale sand.
Ali Hafed also had money saved, and he had lent some of it out at interest. He was a careful man who looked after his affairs.
Best of all, Ali Hafed had a wife and children whom he loved dearly. In the evenings they played in the garden and by the stream.
His days followed the seasons of the whole year on the farm. In spring he ploughed and planted, and in autumn he gathered in the harvest.
In the evenings the family sat down to eat together by lamplight. Ali Hafed looked at their faces and felt like a very lucky man.
In Conwell's telling, Ali Hafed was a man who was both contented and wealthy. He was content because he was wealthy, and wealthy because he was content.
Then, one evening, a visitor came to the farm. His arrival would change everything in Ali Hafed's quiet life.
The visitor was an old priest, a wise man who had studied and travelled widely. Ali Hafed welcomed him warmly and gave him a seat by the fire.
On a cool evening the priest sat by the fire and began to talk. He told Ali Hafed how the world was made.
The priest said that the first diamond was a drop of sunlight that had turned into stone. Ali Hafed had never heard anything so wonderful in all his life.
Today we know that a diamond is made of carbon, the same substance that is found in coal. It forms far underground, under great heat and pressure.
The priest held up his thumb and said that a diamond of that size would buy many farms. Ali Hafed stared at the old man's thumb as if it already shone.
The priest went on to say that a handful of diamonds could buy an entire country. Ali Hafed tried to imagine such a huge fortune.
A whole mine of diamonds, said the priest, could put Ali Hafed's sons on thrones. Their wealth would give them power over whole kingdoms.
That night Ali Hafed went to bed a poor man, although he had lost nothing at all. He was poor only because he wanted more than he had.
Ali Hafed could not sleep that night, however hard he tried. He lay awake and thought about diamonds until the sky began to grow pale.
At dawn Ali Hafed hurried to the priest and woke him from his sleep. He asked the old man to tell him where diamonds could be found.
The tired old priest was not pleased to be woken so early. He asked Ali Hafed why he wanted diamonds so badly.
The priest told him to find a river that runs over white sand between high mountains. In that white sand, he said, there would always be diamonds.
Ali Hafed believed the old priest completely, and without a single doubt. He did not ask for proof, and he did not stop to count the cost.
Ali Hafed sold his farm and gathered all the money that people owed him. He turned everything that he owned into heavy coins.
Ali Hafed left his wife and children in the care of a neighbour. One can imagine the sad farewell at the garden gate.
Then he set off alone with a heavy bag of money on his back. His only plan was to find a river of white sand.
In Conwell's telling, the search began at the Mountains of the Moon. Ancient writers placed these mountains in Africa, at the source of the Nile.
From there he wandered on to Palestine, and later he travelled through Europe. In every country he looked for a river that ran over white sand.
At every river he came to, Ali Hafed stopped and knelt on the bank. He studied the sand, but it was never quite right.
Months went by, and then whole years went by. The money in his purse grew less and less, and still he had found nothing.
Ali Hafed searched the sand of many riverbeds in many different lands. None of them held the diamonds that the priest had described.
He slept outside under the open sky and crossed many lands where nobody knew him. He could not speak the languages that he heard around him.
At long last, the money in his purse was completely gone. He could no longer pay for food, for a bed or for a place on a boat.
He became thin and hungry, and his fine clothes turned to rags. People who passed him on the road thought that he was a beggar.
Sometimes, at night, he thought about his farm, his garden and the children who played in the stream. Those thoughts were sweet to him, but they were also very painful.
He had told himself that he would come home a rich man. He could not bear the thought of going back with nothing in his hands.
At last his road led him to a bay near Barcelona, in Spain. He had come a very long way from the river Indus.
He stood on the shore, worn out and without any hope. Out at sea a great wave was rolling slowly toward the land.
In his deep despair, he gave himself to the great incoming tide. He sank beneath the foaming water and never rose again in this life.
So ended the search of Ali Hafed, far from the home where his riches lay. He had never found a single diamond, and he never would.
Back at the farm on the Indus, the new owner had settled in. He looked after the fields, the orchards and the garden with great care.
One day the new owner led his camel into the garden to drink. He walked down to the little stream where Ali Hafed's children had once played.
The camel lowered its head and put its nose into the shallow water. The stream ran slowly and clearly over its bed of white sand.
When the camel lifted its head, the man noticed a flash of light. It came from the sand at the bottom of the stream.
He reached into the water and pulled out a curious dark stone. It had a bright spot in it that showed all the colours of the rainbow.
He carried the stone into the house and put it on the shelf above the fireplace. Then he went back to his work and forgot all about it.
A few days later the old priest came to visit the new owner. It was the same priest who had once told Ali Hafed about diamonds.
The priest's eye was caught by the flash of light from the shelf. He rushed across the room and cried out, “Here is a diamond!”
Then he asked whether Ali Hafed had come back, and the farmer said that he had not. The farmer added that it was only a stone from the garden.
“I know a diamond when I see one,” said the priest, and he would not be argued with. Together the two men hurried out through the door to the garden stream.
At the stream the two men knelt down and stirred the white sand with their fingers. The priest was trembling with excitement, though the farmer still thought it silly.
Soon they found more stones, and each one seemed more beautiful than the last. Some were larger and brighter than the one on the shelf.
According to the guide, this is how the diamond mine of Golconda was discovered. He said that it was the most magnificent mine in all history.
The real Golconda is in India, near the city of Hyderabad. It was famous for its diamonds for centuries, and the tale simply borrows its name.
Some famous old diamonds, such as the Koh-i-Noor, are said to have come from that part of India. Today the Koh-i-Noor is part of the British crown jewels.
Kimberley, in South Africa, was another great field of diamonds. In the 1870s thousands of diggers dug a huge hole there, almost all of it by hand.
The usual account says that in 1866 a boy found a pretty stone beside a river on a farm in South Africa. Others soon recognised that it was a real diamond.
The guide made his moral plain when he finished the tale. If Ali Hafed had stayed home and dug in his own garden, he would have owned acres of diamonds.
Every shovelful of the old farm, said the guide, would have shown more gems. Those gems later shone in the crowns of kings.
Ali Hafed went hungry and cold in a strange land far away. All the time the treasure lay in the stream where his children had played.
Conwell said that the tale stayed with him long after the journey ended. He turned it over in his mind for years.
Ali Hafed's real trouble was not poverty but discontent. Until the priest spoke, he had been happy; afterward he felt poor, though nothing had changed.
Wanting a better life is not wrong, and Conwell never said that it was. His point is to look at what you already have before you search elsewhere.
The trap is to believe that the good chances are always somewhere else. Far-off places look exciting, while your own street looks ordinary and dull.
Ali Hafed never asked what his own land might hold. It does not seem that anyone ever tested the sand in his garden stream.
Conwell told his listeners that they too were standing in the middle of acres of diamonds. He did not mean that the ground under them was full of jewels.
The diamonds in the tale stand for all kinds of chances in life. They include your skills, your ideas, your friends, your work and the needs of the people around you.
Even in the tale, the diamonds had to be found by someone. The priest and the farmer had to kneel down and stir the sand with their hands.
Sometimes moving away is the right choice for a person. Millions of people have left home to find work, safety or a better school, and the tale does not say they were wrong.
So the useful question is whether you have really looked carefully at the place where you are. It is a question that costs nothing to ask.
Conwell next tells a story from Pennsylvania, in the eastern United States. It is the story of a farm and of the oil beneath it.
In western Pennsylvania, oil had long seeped out of the ground into the creeks. People skimmed it off the water and used it as medicine.
In 1859 Edwin Drake drilled a well near Titusville, Pennsylvania. Oil flowed from about seventy feet down, and the great oil rush began.
In Conwell's telling, one farmer sold his farm and went far away to hunt for oil. He did not think to look closely at his own land.
The new owner noticed a dark film on the farm stream. He put a board across the water to hold it back so that his cattle could drink.
In the story, that farm lay above one of the richest oil fields in the region. The oil had been there all along, and nobody had looked.
In January 1848 a carpenter named James Marshall found shining flakes in the millrace of Sutter's Mill, in California. The flakes proved to be real gold, and the news spread fast.
The news of the gold raced around the whole world. By about 1855, some three hundred thousand people had come to California by ship and by wagon.
Few people grew rich by digging for gold, and many went home with little. Some stayed on and became farmers, merchants or craftsmen.
Shopkeepers who sold tools, food and clothes often did better than the diggers. The first finder was not a traveller but a worker already on the spot.
Conwell's first rule is not to wait for a better time or a better place. Opportunity, he says, is found where you stand today, not elsewhere.
He asked his listeners to think about the people around them. What do your neighbours lack, and what would they gladly pay for?
It is said that before each talk Conwell studied the town he was visiting. He asked questions about its shops, its factories and its people.
Think of a town with a school, a mill and a railway station. The school needs books, the mill needs workers, and the station needs people to carry goods.
Moving away rarely cures a worry, because you take yourself along with you. A new town brings new problems along with its new chances.
You know your own town, your neighbours and their customs. A stranger who arrives tomorrow knows none of these things at all.
Your neighbours already know your name, your family and your character. Trust is slow to build, so you start far ahead of any newcomer.
Starting again in a new place costs money, and trust must be earned all over again. Staying where you are saves both of these costs.
Conwell did not mean that people should sit still and wait. He meant that they should begin today, with what is in front of them.
Here is a simple way to try the idea for yourself. Write down five things that people in your street lack or often complain about.
Conwell's rule for finding the diamond is to find out what people need. Then you supply it, and people pay you for your trouble.
People pay for things that help them, not for things that the maker happens to like. A fine product that nobody needs will sit on the shelf.
In 1854 Elisha Otis showed a safety brake for lifts at the New York Crystal Palace. It made tall buildings much safer to use, and it was used in many cities.
Margaret Knight worked in a paper-bag factory and invented a machine to make flat-bottomed bags. She won a patent for her machine in the year 1871.
Josephine Cochrane wanted to protect her good dishes from careless hands. In 1886 she patented a machine that washed them for her.
A tailor named Jacob Davis put metal rivets in work trousers so that the pockets would not tear. With the help of Levi Strauss, he gained a patent in 1873.
Each of these people began with one small, real problem. They noticed it, they thought about it, and then they did something.
Ask what people near you find hard, and what wastes their time. Ask also what they already pay other people to do.
Not everyone has to invent a machine in order to meet a need. Teaching, cooking, mending and caring for others all meet real needs too.
Learning what people really need takes patience and careful attention. You must watch closely, ask questions and listen to the answers.
Conwell says to start small, right where you are, with what you already have. Big plans can wait until the first small step works.
A good start needs attention more than it needs cash. Many useful ideas cost very little to try, if you watch closely.
Many firms began in a kitchen, in a shed or in a corner of a shop. Their owners had little space, but they had a clear idea.
A small start lets you learn cheaply, because early mistakes cost little. A mistake in a small trade is a lesson, and a mistake in a large one can be a disaster.
Your first customers are likely to be your own neighbours. If they are pleased with you, they tell their friends, and your name begins to spread.
Put aside a little money each week, even when the amount seems tiny. A small saving is a seed that can grow into a tool or a shop.
Levi Strauss opened a dry-goods business in San Francisco in 1853. It started small, and over the years it grew into a famous firm.
Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a small bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio. In that shop they built the machine that made the first powered flights in 1903.
When one small step works, you should take the next one. Do not try to leap to the top of the stairs in a single jump, because you may fall.
Conwell's advice can be put into three very simple steps. Find a real need, plan a way to meet it, and begin.
Your own skills, your friends and your surroundings are your acres of diamonds. They are already yours, and you do not have to buy them.
Learning and practising a skill makes you more useful to others. A person who is really useful to others is always in demand.
This is why Conwell started evening classes for working people. He saw learning as a way of digging for the treasure inside every person.
Benjamin Franklin learned the printing trade as a boy, working for his older brother. He also read as many books as he could find.
A skill is built by steady practice, a little each day. Nobody becomes truly skilled in the course of a single week.
A farmer knows that there is no shortcut to a good harvest. Seeds must be planted, watered and weeded before anything grows.
Distant fields always look much greener than our own fields do. Ali Hafed's story warns us against envy of faraway things.
Begin by serving the people who are nearest to you. That means your family, your neighbours and the people of your town.
Friends and neighbours are part of the treasure too, so do not neglect them. They may offer you good advice, honest work or a useful introduction.
A person who is truly useful has a kind of safety in life. There is always some work for someone who can do something well.
Conwell said that it is right, and even a duty, to become rich honestly. He added that the money should be used for a good purpose.
Conwell thought that many good people avoid wealth because they believe that wanting money is wrong. He said that this belief holds them back from doing good.
Conwell pointed out that the Bible warns against the love of money. It does not, he said, warn against money itself.
A person who is honest and serves customers well earns their trust. Trust brings customers back to the same shop again and again.
Conwell claimed that most rich people had earned their money honestly. Yet in his own time, the Gilded Age, some large fortunes were made by cheating.
A good name takes many years of honest work to build up. One dishonest act can spoil it in a single day.
Conwell held a hard view that many readers find unkind today. He believed that most poor people were poor through their own faults.
Many people today see more causes of poverty than personal fault. They include illness, bad luck, low pay and unequal chances.
Still, Conwell believed in helping people who were trying to improve their lives. Much of his own money went to help students pay for school.
So honest effort is a good thing and worth admiring. But we should not judge people who are poor too quickly or too harshly.
Conwell said that money is a power that can do much good. It can pay for schools, churches, hospitals and homes for those in need.
Stephen Girard, a rich banker in Philadelphia, left money for a school for poor orphan boys. The school, Girard College, opened in 1848, many years after his death.
Peter Cooper was a New York businessman who built useful things and made a fortune. In 1859 he opened Cooper Union, which gave free education to working people.
When Benjamin Franklin died in 1790, he left money to Philadelphia and to Boston. It was to be lent to young craftsmen who wanted to start a trade.
Conwell asked those who grow rich to give wisely, and not only to keep. He believed that wealth carries a duty to help other people.
You do not need to be rich in order to give to other people. Your time, your skill and your care are valuable gifts too.
The danger comes when money stops being a tool and becomes a master. Then a person works only for coins and forgets everything else.
Ali Hafed already had enough, but after the priest's visit he could no longer see it. Knowing what is enough is itself a kind of wealth.
Wealth is not only money, and Conwell's tale shows it clearly. Health, family, friends, good work and a good name all count as riches too.
At the start of the tale, Ali Hafed had every one of these riches. He left them all behind for the sake of a dream.
Greatness, Conwell says, is not a matter of fame or of high office. It is the habit of doing great good in plain and ordinary places.
A good teacher in a small school can change many lives. Such a person rarely gets a statue or a newspaper headline.
Abraham Lincoln was born in 1809 in a log cabin in Kentucky. He had very little schooling, yet he became the president of the United States.
Conwell himself was a boy from a hill farm in a small town. Nothing in his early life promised that he would speak to crowds in great cities.
Many people who do great good come from small towns and plain homes. You do not need to be famous in order to be one of them.
Every famous person was once a neighbour whom few people knew. Their first steps were taken in plain places, without any cheering.
You can show real greatness in small and everyday things. A kind act, a fair price and a kept promise are all good examples.
A person who serves a community faithfully becomes known for it. In time, such a person is often trusted with larger duties.
Fame is quick to fade, and Ali Hafed once longed for thrones. But a useful life leaves something lasting behind it.
Greatness is open to everyone who is willing to listen. It can begin today, in your own street, with a single useful act.
The lecture belongs to the time in which Conwell lived and spoke. Enjoy its plain wisdom, but weigh its opinions and its facts with care.
Times have changed, and chances were never equal for everyone. In Conwell's day, many women and many Black Americans faced barriers that hard digging could not remove.
Where barriers are real, people have often worked together to change them. They have built schools, formed unions and won the right to vote.
Here is the whole lecture, in short, boiled down to four ideas. Find a need, serve it honestly, build a skill and work steadily.
Conwell hopes that those who succeed will use their money for good. He also hopes that they will be content with a useful life.
Ali Hafed is not a villain, and nobody in the tale is. He is only a man who looked past what he already had.
The tale of Ali Hafed has been retold in many books, sermons and speeches. Many people who have never read the lecture know its story.
When you close the book, look at your own street as a stranger would. You may see chances that you never noticed before.
Before you go, try writing three short lists on a single sheet of paper. One should hold your skills, one the people you know, and one the needs near you.
So ask yourself where your own acres of diamonds might be. The answer may be in your town, your work, your skills, or even your own back garden.
C1C2: The hall is full to the last seat, and the murmur of the crowd dies away as a tall man in a dark suit walks to the front. Russell Conwell has done this many times before, yet he speaks as though each listener were a new friend. The talk he is about to give, called Acres of Diamonds, became one of the most often repeated speeches in American history.

Few speakers have repeated one lecture as often as Conwell repeated Acres of Diamonds. By most counts he gave it thousands of times over many years, and some people say more than six thousand. It is said that he changed small parts each time to suit the audience in front of him.

In the age of the steam railway a speaker could cross a country in a few days, and Conwell used the trains to carry his talk to places both large and small. Ordinary people, farmers, clerks and shopkeepers among them, filled the seats of town halls and churches. Because he went to the people instead of waiting for them to come, his words reached crowds that no city hall could ever have held.

This book began its life as a voice, and not as words on a page. Conwell spoke the lecture over and over, and it was printed only afterwards, so the words carry the warmth and the plain, friendly rhythm of a man talking to a crowd. That is why it feels more like a conversation with a wise neighbour than a lesson from a teacher's desk.

An acre is a measure of land, roughly the size of a football field, and Conwell's title asks us to imagine not one diamond but whole fields of them. The picture is deliberately extravagant, a treasure so vast that nobody could carry it away in a pocket. It is meant to make us wonder how much value may be lying around us, unnoticed.

To the people who filled Conwell's halls, a diamond was the very picture of riches, small enough to hold in one hand and worth a fortune. It is the hardest natural substance known, it is made deep in the earth over an immense span of time, and it is found in only a few places. No wonder it made such a perfect symbol for a treasure that everyone longs to own.

The plan of the lecture is as plain as a path through a garden. It opens with a tale about a farmer and a search for treasure, moves on to what that tale means for ordinary lives, and ends with practical advice that any listener could try the next morning. Each step leads naturally to the next, and we shall follow them in the same order.

The central claim of the lecture can be stated in a single breath: the chance you are looking for may be lying at your own feet. Conwell did not promise that it would be easy to see, or that it would come without effort. He argued only that it was far more likely to be near than far, and that most of us have not looked near enough.

Conwell's audiences were not scholars or kings but working people, men and women with jobs, families and a quiet longing to do a little better. To them he offered neither magic nor luck but a new way of looking at the place where they already lived. That may be a large part of why so many wanted to hear the same talk again and again.

A tale is always a little different in the mouth of the one who tells it, and this tale is Conwell's through and through. Before we follow Ali Hafed along his long and winding road, it is worth learning who Conwell was and what shaped him. His own life, as we shall discover, took more unexpected turns than many a novel.

Russell Conwell was born in 1843 on a farm in the hills of western Massachusetts, near the small village of South Worthington. It was a place of stone walls, short summers and long winters, where children learned early that nothing came without work. The boy who grew up there would one day tell crowds in great cities that opportunity can be found in the humblest place.

The farm could feed a boy, but it could not satisfy his hunger for learning, and Conwell set his heart on a life of study. He went away to school and then to Yale, one of the oldest and best-known colleges in America. It was a long way from the hill farm, and it showed him that a person's beginnings need not fix his road.

In 1861 the American Civil War broke out, and young men all over the North put down their books and picked up rifles. Conwell was among them, and he served in the Union army and became an officer who led a company of soldiers. The war taught him a great deal about courage, hardship and the quiet worth of ordinary men.

When the fighting was over, Conwell looked for a new way to serve and settled on the law. He studied at the law school in Albany, in the state of New York, and learned how courts, contracts and quarrels between neighbours are put right. It was a practical education, and he would draw on it for the rest of his life.

Conwell opened a law office in Minneapolis, which was then a young and growing city, and later he moved back east to work as a lawyer in Boston. In both places he met all kinds of people, from careful shopkeepers to anxious borrowers, and he heard their troubles at first hand. Such meetings gave him an unusual understanding of how people succeed and fail with money.

Alongside his work in the law he wrote for newspapers, and that writing sent him on long journeys through Europe, the Middle East and Asia. He saw ancient cities and brand-new ones, crowded markets and empty deserts, and he came home with a head full of stories. One of those stories, he said, was handed to him by a guide on the banks of a famous river.

In 1879, after years in other trades, Conwell took up the work that would shape the rest of his life and became a Baptist minister. His first church stood in Lexington, Massachusetts, a small town near Boston, and the congregation there was modest in size. He accepted the post all the same, and he is remembered for the energy he brought to it.

Three years later, in 1882, Conwell accepted a call to a small church in Philadelphia, and the congregation soon found the little building too full to hold everyone who came. Word spread that the new minister spoke plainly, helped his neighbours and welcomed all comers. Within a few years the crowds were far too large for the room that was meant to hold them.

So many people came that the congregation decided to build something much larger, and the result was the Baptist Temple, one of the largest churches of its day. It opened in 1891 and stood in the middle of a busy city, with room for thousands. It was a fitting stage for a minister whose fame was spreading far beyond the city.

Conwell was also a prolific writer, and over the years his pen produced many books, among them the life stories of well-known leaders of his time. Few people have filled so many roles in a single lifetime, as a soldier, a lawyer, a traveller, a minister and an author. Each of them gave him a different window onto the way ordinary people live.

One evening in 1884 a young man came to Conwell with a very bold request. He lacked the time and the money for college, but he wished to become a minister, and he asked whether Conwell would teach him. Conwell agreed, and that quiet decision set a great chain of events in motion.

Word soon spread, and other working men and women asked to join the lessons, bringing their notebooks after a long day of labour. Conwell did not turn them away, and the little group began to meet regularly in the evenings. It was a modest start, but it was the seed of something much larger.

The evening classes grew year by year, and in time the school needed a name, a charter and teachers beyond Conwell himself. It was called Temple College, after the Baptist Temple where it had first begun. From a handful of tired workers in a church room, it had become a proper institution.

Conwell is said to have given a large share of what he earned from his lectures to the school, so that every audience he addressed helped to pay for the teaching of working students. In this way a talk about hidden treasure was turned into books, desks and teachers. It was the lecture's own advice, quietly put to work in the real world.

The great advantage of the school was that its students could work by day and study by night, and so no one was asked to choose between earning a living and improving his mind. Clerks, shop assistants, factory workers and mothers sat side by side in the evening classes. For many of them it opened a door that would otherwise have stayed firmly shut.

His concern for his neighbours reached beyond the classroom, and Conwell also helped to found the Samaritan Hospital in Philadelphia, which cared for the sick whether or not they could pay. In later years it grew into part of the hospital that belongs to the university. A man who had once been a soldier and a lawyer now found himself building places of healing and learning.

In 1907 the college won the right to call itself a university, and it has kept growing ever since. Today Temple is a large university with thousands of students from many countries, and its history is rooted in a few evening lessons given to a young man. Few schools can trace their beginnings so precisely to a single act of generosity.

Conwell led the school for the rest of his long life, balancing the care of a college, a church and a hospital with his endless travels as a speaker. He died in 1925 at the age of eighty-two, and by then the evening class that began with a single student had become a centre of learning. Even those who disagreed with his opinions could see plainly what he had built.

The story of the school is, in a way, the whole lecture lived out in practice. Conwell saw a need in the people around him, he began in a small way with a single student and a single room, and he used the gifts he already possessed, his learning and his voice. He did not travel to the ends of the earth to find his diamond, for it was waiting in his own church.

Now we come to the part of the lecture that every listener remembered long after the rest had faded. It begins far from Philadelphia and far from the world of churches and classrooms, on the banks of a slow, wide river in the Middle East. There a young traveller is about to hear a story that he will never forget.

As a young man Conwell journeyed through the Middle East, and his road took him along the Tigris and Euphrates, the two great rivers of what is now Iraq. Their valley is often called Mesopotamia, a name that means the land between the rivers. Some of the oldest cities in the world once rose beside their muddy banks.

In the city of Baghdad, Conwell hired a guide to lead him to the ruins of ancient places such as Babylon, whose great walls and gardens were famous in the old world.
