The guide knew the roads, the villages and the dusty histories of the land as well as he knew his own hand. He was the ideal companion for a curious young traveller with time to listen.

Travel in that country was slow, and the party moved at the pace of the camels that carried their baggage across the dusty plains. The sun was hot, the road was long, and the landscape changed so little that there was nothing to do but talk. In such conditions a good storyteller is a precious companion, worth more than a cool breeze.

The guide was a man who loved the sound of his own voice, and he seemed to have a tale ready for every bend in the river and every pile of old stones. Many of them, one imagines, were about kings and battles, and some were about buried treasure. Conwell listened to them all with the patience of a man who is far from home.

One day, as the camels plodded on, the guide offered to tell a tale that was a favourite of his own. It concerned a Persian farmer who lived beside the river Indus long ago, and it began quietly enough. Conwell, who had heard many stories already, had no idea that this one would stay with him for the rest of his life.

Nobody can say for certain whether the tale is an ancient legend or a clever invention, and it may well be a mixture of both. Folk tales travel from mouth to mouth across the centuries, and each storyteller changes a detail here and adds a flourish there. What matters most is not where this particular tale came from, but what it has to teach.

Persia is the old name of the country now called Iran, and in ancient times the Persian empire reached as far east as the river Indus. That river rises in the mountains of Tibet and flows for more than three thousand kilometres through Pakistan to the Arabian Sea. A Persian farmer by the Indus, then, was not a strange idea at all.

The farmer in the guide's tale was named Ali Hafed, and he lived on the banks of the Indus, far to the east of the place where Conwell sat listening. He was not a king or a soldier but an ordinary working man with an ordinary life. That is exactly why the story speaks so well to ordinary listeners in ordinary towns.

Conwell never forgot the guide's tale, and he kept it in his memory for years until he was ready to use it. When he became a speaker, he made it the opening of his lecture and told it, in his own words, to crowds all over America. It became, by a wide margin, the best-known story that he ever told to anyone.

So let us pause beside the river at dusk, while the camels rest and the sun goes down, and listen to the guide. It is a tale about a man who had almost everything he could wish for and did not know it, and about the long road he took to find that out. The story begins, as many of the best stories do, in a quiet and peaceful place.

Ali Hafed lived on a large and prosperous farm beside the river Indus, and in the tale he wanted for nothing that a farmer could reasonably desire. His land was wide, his work was steady, and his mind was at peace. In the words of the tale, he was a contented man, and he knew it.

His broad fields of grain rippled like water in the summer wind, and when the harvest came, the barns were filled to the roof. Ali Hafed and his household cut, bound and stored the crop with the quiet pride of people who know their land. There was always enough to eat, and often a good deal more than enough to share with friends.

Beyond the fields stood his orchards, rows of trees that bent under the weight of ripe fruit in the warm season. Branches reached down almost to the grass, and the air was sweet with the smell of the harvest. Ali Hafed walked slowly among them in the cool of the evening, a man at peace with the world and glad of every tree.

Beside the house lay a garden, and through the garden ran a small, clear stream that murmured over beds of pale sand. It was a pleasant, ordinary thing, and no one who looked at it would have thought it worth a second glance. Ali Hafed certainly never did, and that is a part of the tale to remember.

Besides land, Ali Hafed owned a store of money, and he had lent a part of it out at interest, so that it quietly grew while he slept. He was careful with his affairs, being neither a spendthrift who wasted money nor a miser who hoarded it. In short, he was a comfortable and sensible man, well established in his neighbourhood.

Best of all, Ali Hafed had a wife and children whom he loved dearly, and their laughter filled the house from morning until night. The children played in the garden and splashed in the little stream, and they were healthy and well fed. No king in the whole world could have asked for a richer or a happier household than his.

The rhythm of his days was set by the seasons, with ploughing and planting in the spring, watering through the long summer, and the great gathering of the harvest in autumn. It was hard work, but it was honest work, and it gave him a good appetite and a good night's sleep. Year after year the pattern repeated itself, and year after year it rewarded him with plenty and peace.

When the work was done, the family gathered round the table by lamplight and shared the day's bread, and Ali Hafed looked at the faces around him with a full heart. He thought himself a fortunate man, and in the plainest sense he was right. Whatever else the tale would teach, it began with a man who truly had enough.

In Conwell's telling, Ali Hafed was both a contented man and a wealthy one, and the two went hand in hand. He was content because he was wealthy, and wealthy because he was content, each blessing feeding the other. Hold on to that thought, for the story is about what happens when one of the two goes missing.

Then, one evening at sunset, a visitor appeared at the gate of the farm, leaning on a stick and wrapped in a travelling cloak. He was no stranger to Ali Hafed, but the words he carried would soon turn a peaceful household upside down. Nothing had been lost yet and nothing had been stolen, but the quiet contentment of the farm was about to end.

The visitor was an old priest, a man known for his learning, who had studied the ways of the world and the stars above it. Ali Hafed welcomed him warmly into his house, as a good host should, and offered him a place by the fire. Neither could have guessed that the conversation of that night would cost the farmer everything he owned.

It was a cool evening, and the priest sat close to the fire, warming his thin hands, while the family listened. He began to tell Ali Hafed how the world had been made, in the old story of mist and fire and cooling stone. The farmer, who had never given the matter much thought, found himself drawn in by the tale.

Among the first of the earth's treasures, said the priest, was the diamond, which he described as a drop of sunlight that had hardened into stone. It was a beautiful picture, and Ali Hafed turned it over in his mind as a child turns a bright pebble in his hand. He had never before thought of the light on his own fields as something that might be kept.

The scientific truth about diamonds is less poetic than the priest's picture, though it is no less wonderful. A diamond is a form of carbon, the same element that is found in coal and in pencil lead, and it is created deep underground, under enormous heat and pressure, over a span of time that dwarfs human history. Volcanic eruptions then carry some of these stones up toward the surface, where people can find them.

To show how precious such a stone could be, the priest held up his thumb and declared that a diamond of that size could buy a whole district full of farms. Ali Hafed looked at his own farm, which had always seemed to him a great estate, and suddenly it seemed rather small. A single glittering stone, it appeared, was worth more than all his fields and orchards put together.

Then the old man went further and said that a handful of such stones would be enough to purchase an entire country, with its cities, its armies and its kings. The farmer, who had thought himself comfortably rich, now felt like a child who has been shown the sea for the first time. The conversation had only just begun, and already the comfortable evening was slipping away.

With a whole mine of diamonds, said the priest, a man could set his sons upon thrones through the influence of their immense wealth. He painted the picture in glowing words, and Ali Hafed, who loved his children, saw each of them wearing a crown. It was a dazzling dream, and dreams of that kind do not sit quietly in a person's head.

When the priest had finished, Ali Hafed went to bed that night a poor man, though he had lost nothing whatever. He was poor only because he was discontented, and he was discontented because he now felt that he was poor. Here, in one small circle of thought, is the real sickness that runs through the whole tale.

Ali Hafed lay awake in the dark, staring at the ceiling, while his wife and children slept peacefully nearby. His farm, his orchards and his garden had not changed in the least, but they no longer seemed to him enough. Hour after hour the thought of diamonds went round and round in his head, until the sky began to grow pale.

As soon as the first grey light appeared, Ali Hafed rose, hurried to the priest's bedside and woke the old man from a deep sleep. He could not wait for breakfast or for a more civil hour, for the question had been burning inside him all night. He asked, in a trembling voice, where a man might go to find diamonds.

The old priest, who had been sleeping soundly, was not at all pleased to be woken at such an hour. He frowned and asked what a man with a good farm could possibly want with diamonds. Ali Hafed answered that he wished to be immensely rich, and that nothing else would content him.

Rather impatiently, the old man told Ali Hafed to go out and find a river that runs over white sand between high mountains. In the white sand of such a river, he said, a man would always find diamonds. It was the vaguest of directions, and it was enough to send a farmer round the world.

Ali Hafed believed the old priest completely and without the slightest doubt, and he thanked him warmly. He did not ask how many people had tried and failed, he did not ask whether the river even existed, and he did not stop to ask what a search might cost him. When a dream has taken hold of a man's heart, as the tale shows, it leaves little room for questions.

Ali Hafed lost no time at all in turning his whole prosperous life into ready money. He sold the farm, with its fields, orchards and garden, and he collected every coin that he had lent out at interest. In a few days a household that had stood for years was reduced to a heavy purse.

He left his wife and children in the care of a neighbour, promising that he would return with riches beyond measure. One can picture the family at the garden gate, the children waving and the mother wiping her eyes. He walked away down the road, certain that he was doing the best thing for them.

With a bag of money over his shoulder and a head full of dreams, he set off alone along the road that led away from the Indus. His only plan was to find a river that ran over white sand between high mountains. How hard could it be, he must have thought, to find a single river in the whole wide world?

In Conwell's telling, Ali Hafed began his search, quite properly, at the Mountains of the Moon, a range of old legend which ancient writers placed in Africa, near the source of the Nile. It was a long way from the Indus, and he must have crossed deserts and seas to reach it. If any mountains were high enough for the priest's river, surely these were the ones.

From the mountains he wandered on to Palestine, and later he made his way through country after country in Europe, always asking and always looking. Each new land brought him new rivers, strange languages, unfamiliar customs and fresh disappointments of every kind. In the tale, the more places he visited, the further he seemed to be from his goal.

At every river that he crossed, Ali Hafed stopped, knelt on the bank and scooped up a handful of sand to study. Sometimes the sand was yellow, sometimes it was grey, and sometimes the mountains were too low or the water too muddy. The perfect river, the one the priest had described, kept slipping out of his reach.

Months went by, then years, and the heavy purse that had weighed on his shoulder grew lighter with every town and every meal. He paid for boats, for bread and for a bed in a hundred strange inns. Still the diamonds he had dreamed of seemed to be as far away from him as they had ever been.

He sifted the sand of riverbeds in one country after another, using his hands, a pan and a great deal of patience. None of them held the diamonds that the priest had promised, and none of them was quite the river he had been told to find. Each failure only made him more determined, and that determination was slowly eating him up.

Night after night he slept in the open, wrapped in his cloak, in places where no one knew his name and no one cared. He crossed borders and mountains, and he could rarely make himself understood in the languages he met. For a man who had once sat at the head of his own table, it was a hard and lonely life.

At last the day came when he turned his purse upside down and not a single coin fell out. He could no longer pay for food, for a bed or for a place on a boat, and the road ahead was all the harder for it. The man who had once lent money to his neighbours now had nothing to lend and nothing to spend.

He grew thin and hungry, and the fine clothes in which he had left the Indus gradually fell to rags. People who passed him on the road took him for a beggar, and some of them would not even look him in the face. It was a sad change for a man who had once owned orchards and gardens.

Sometimes, in the long dark hours, his mind went back to the farm, the orchard, the table by lamplight and the children who played in the garden stream. Such memories were sweet to him, and bitter too, for they showed him exactly what he had given away. He pushed them aside and walked on, telling himself that the next river would be the right one.

He had told himself that he would come home a rich man, bringing gifts for his wife and crowns for his sons. To return with empty hands, poor and ashamed, was more than his pride could bear. So, weary but obstinate, he turned his face once more toward the distant horizon and trudged on.

In the end his long road led him to the coast of Spain, to a bay near the city of Barcelona, where the hills run down to the Mediterranean Sea. He had come thousands of miles from the Indus, and he had found nothing but hunger and fatigue. His strength was spent, his money was gone and his hope was almost gone as well.

He stood alone on the shore, worn out in body and in spirit, looking at the sea as though it might have an answer for him. Out beyond the harbour a great wave was gathering itself, rolling steadily in toward the land. Behind him lay the long road, and before him lay nothing but the grey water.

In that moment the poor, tired man could not resist the terrible temptation, and he gave himself to the incoming tide. He sank beneath the foaming crest of the wave and did not rise again in this life. The tale does not dwell on the sadness, and neither shall we, but it does not hide it either.

So ended the search of Ali Hafed, in a foreign land, far from the farm where his true riches had lain all the time. He had surrendered his home, his savings and at last his life, and he had not found a single stone. The next part of the tale turns back to the very place that he had abandoned so hastily.

Meanwhile, back at the farm beside the Indus, the man who had bought it from Ali Hafed had settled in and gone to work. He tended the fields, the orchards and the garden with care, as any sensible owner would. He did not know that he was living on top of the greatest treasure in the land.

One day the new owner led his camel into the garden so that it could drink from the little stream that ran through it. It was an ordinary errand on an ordinary day, and he thought no more about it than he thought about breakfast. The sun was warm, the water was clear, and nothing in the scene suggested that it was about to become famous.

The camel lowered its long neck and put its nose into the shallow water, which ran slowly and clearly over a bed of white sand. The man stood by with the rope in his hand, idly watching the ripples spread. It was, in fact, just the kind of white sand that Ali Hafed had crossed half the world to find.

As the camel lifted its head, the man noticed a sudden flash of light flickering among the grains of sand at the bottom of the stream. He looked closer, for something in that small gleam seemed quite unlike an ordinary pebble. The sun had caught it, and it threw back the light as though it were alive.

He reached down into the cool water and drew out a curious dark pebble with an eye of light in its heart. When he turned it in his fingers, the spot flashed with every colour of the rainbow, red and gold and green and blue. It was certainly a pretty thing, and he did not know what else to say about it.

Pleased with his pretty find, he carried it into the house and set it on the shelf above the fireplace. Then he went back to his work in the fields and soon forgot all about it. Such stones, he supposed, were not uncommon, and a busy farmer had many more pressing matters to attend to.

A few days later an old visitor arrived at the farm, and it was the very same priest who had once told Ali Hafed about diamonds. He had come to call on the new owner, as such men do, and to see how the old farm was doing. He strode into the house, glanced idly around the room, and then stopped dead in the middle of the floor, staring.

The old man's eye was caught at once by the flash of light from the shelf above the fireplace, and he hurried across the room as fast as his years would allow. He stared at the stone for a long moment in astonished silence, and then he cried out that it was a diamond. His voice rang through the quiet house like a bell, and the farmer jumped.

Then the priest inquired whether Ali Hafed had returned, and the new owner replied that nobody had set eyes on him since the day he left. The farmer added that the stone was nothing remarkable, merely a pebble that he had picked out of his own garden. He could not for the life of him understand why the old man was in such a state of excitement.

“I know a diamond when I see one,” said the priest firmly, and he would not hear another word of argument. Taking the farmer by the arm, he pulled him toward the door, and together the two men hurried out into the garden. Behind them, on the shelf above the empty hearth, the little stone went on glittering quietly in the half dark.

At the stream the two men knelt side by side on the bank and began to stir the white sand with their fingers, while the camel looked on in mild surprise. The priest's hands trembled with excitement, though the farmer still thought the whole thing rather silly. Neither of them said a word as the sand swirled and settled in the clear water.

It was not long before their fingers closed on a second stone and then a third, and each seemed more beautiful and more valuable than the one before. Some were larger than the pebble on the shelf, and others flashed with a fire that made the farmer gasp. The humble garden stream, it was now perfectly clear, was lined from end to end with precious jewels.

According to the guide, this was how the diamond mine of Golconda was discovered, the most magnificent mine in the whole history of mankind. He claimed that it surpassed even the great fields of Kimberley, and that its stones had gone to decorate the crowns of the world's most powerful rulers. A story told from the back of a camel is surely allowed a little grandeur, and the guide made the most of it.

The real Golconda lies in India, near the city of Hyderabad, where a great fortress stands on a rocky hill above the plain. For centuries the region was famous for its diamonds, which were traded to merchants and rulers across the world, and the tale simply borrows its glamorous name. As far as anyone knows, no diamond mine has ever been found in a Persian farmer's garden.

Some of the most famous old diamonds in the world, among them the Koh-i-Noor, are said to have come from that part of India. The Koh-i-Noor now belongs to the British crown jewels, and several countries still argue over who should rightly own it. Its long history of kings, wars and quarrels is a real story, and quite as dramatic as any legend.

Kimberley, in South Africa, became the centre of the world's diamond trade after diamonds were found there around 1871. Thousands of diggers rushed to the spot, and with picks and shovels they dug a vast crater, now called the Big Hole, almost entirely by hand. It is said to be the largest hole ever dug by hand, and the guide used it as the yardstick of a truly rich mine.

The usual account of the first African discovery sounds uncannily like the guide's tale of the camel and the stone. In 1866 a young boy picked up a pretty stone beside a river on his family's farm in South Africa, and it was later recognised as a diamond. Within a few years the news had drawn thousands of hopeful diggers to the region.

When the tale was finished at last, the guide drew the moral plainly for his young listener. Had Ali Hafed stayed at home and dug in his own garden, instead of wandering to starvation and death in a strange land, he would have had acres of diamonds. That, in a single sentence, is where the title of the lecture comes from.

Every shovelful of that old farm, the guide said, would have uncovered more of the gems that went on to decorate the crowns of monarchs. Each acre was a treasury waiting to be opened by anyone with a spade and a little curiosity. And the man who had once owned it all had turned his back on it and walked away.

While Ali Hafed went hungry in a strange land, the treasure he longed for lay in the little stream where his children had splashed and played. He had walked past it a thousand times and watched his family laugh beside it. It is hard to imagine a crueller irony, and it is the very heart of the tale.

Conwell said that the guide's tale stayed with him long after the camels and the river had been left behind. He turned it over in his mind for years, as one turns over a coin to see both sides, and each time it seemed to say something new. In the end he decided that it was not really a tale about diamonds at all.

In Conwell's view, Ali Hafed's real trouble was never poverty, which he did not have, but discontent, which he caught like a fever from a single conversation. Until the priest spoke he had been perfectly happy, and afterward he felt miserably poor, although not one thing on his farm had changed. The farm was exactly the same as before; only his way of seeing it had altered, and that alone was enough to ruin his peace.

Wanting a better life is not wrong, and Conwell never claimed that it was; ambition drove him as hard as anyone. His point is a narrower one, that before you set out across the world you should look carefully at the ground you are standing on. A search that begins at home costs little, and it may save a lifetime of wandering.

The trap is the belief that the good chances are always somewhere else, in another town, another trade or another country. Far-off places look exciting precisely because we do not know them, while our own street looks dull because we know it too well. Familiarity, in other words, can hide a treasure from our eyes quite as effectively as any distance can.

Not once, so far as the tale tells, did Ali Hafed stop to ask what his own land might hold, or to look closely at the sand in his garden stream. He had trusted a priest's word about the world far away and had never questioned his own ignorance of the world nearby. A little curiosity at home, a spade and an afternoon in the garden would have cost him nothing at all.

Then Conwell turned to the faces in front of him and told his listeners that they, too, were standing in the middle of their own acres of diamonds. He did not mean that the ground beneath the hall was full of jewels, but that every person there was surrounded by chances that they had not yet noticed. It was a bold thing to say to a room full of strangers, and it is easy to see why it held their attention.

In the lecture the diamonds stand for opportunities of every kind, such as a skill you have learned, an idea you have had or a friend who might help you. They include the work that is waiting at your own door and the needs of the neighbours whom you meet every day. Most of us own a good many of them already, and most of us have simply never counted.

Conwell never suggested that the treasure would simply leap into a person's hand, and even in the tale the diamonds had to be found. The priest and the farmer had to kneel in the stream, stir the sand with their fingers and look closely at what came up. Opportunity, in other words, is something to be worked for, and not merely waited for.

It would be a mistake to read the tale as an order never to leave home. Millions of people have moved to find work, safety, education or freedom, and many of them were right to go, as any history of migration shows. The lesson of the tale is not that leaving is foolish, but that leaving without first looking around is a gamble.

So the question that Conwell leaves with us is a simple one, and it can be asked by anyone, anywhere, at any age: have I really looked carefully at the place where I am? If the answer is no, then the search for diamonds has not yet begun, whatever journeys we may have made. The chapters that follow are, in a sense, a practical guide to looking, and they begin with two famous examples from history.

Conwell next gives his audience a story closer to home, set on a farm in Pennsylvania, the state where many of his listeners lived. As he tells it, the farm was owned by a man who wanted to find oil, and he looked everywhere except under his own feet. It is Ali Hafed's story again, set in a different land and told in a different dress.

In western Pennsylvania, black oil had long seeped from the rocks into the creeks, and people had known about it for generations. They skimmed it from the surface of the water with cloths and blankets, and some sold it as a medicine for aches and pains. Nobody yet imagined that it might become the foundation of a vast new industry.

In 1859 a man named Edwin Drake drilled a well near Titusville, in Pennsylvania, and struck oil at a depth of about seventy feet. His success astonished the neighbourhood, and within a few years the valleys were crowded with wooden towers, storage tanks and hopeful investors. The oil rush had begun, and it went on to change the American economy.

In Conwell's telling, a farmer in that part of the country sold his farm for a modest sum and went off to hunt for oil in some distant place. He was certain that the fortune must be waiting somewhere else, and he never thought to look closely at his own fields. So off he went, and he took all of his hopes and every one of his dreams along with him.

The man who bought the farm soon noticed a dark, oily film floating on the stream that crossed it. Being practical, he laid a board across the water to hold back the scum, so that his cattle could drink from the clean water behind it. The first owner had seen that same dark film every day of his life, and he had never once asked what it might mean.

In the story, the farm lay directly above one of the richest oil fields in the region, and the new owner grew wealthy from it. The treasure that the first owner had travelled so far to find had been seeping into his own stream, in plain view, for years. The lesson is the same as in the Persian tale, and the stakes are just as large.

In January 1848 a carpenter named James Marshall noticed shining flakes in the water of a millrace at Sutter's Mill, beside the American River in California. He was building a sawmill for his employer, John Sutter, and he had not set out to look for treasure at all. The flakes turned out to be gold, and the news was soon impossible to keep quiet.

The news raced around the world, and in the following years people poured into California by ship, by wagon and on foot, in a great movement known as the gold rush. By about 1855 some three hundred thousand people had arrived, many of them having left homes, farms and families thousands of miles away. Those who arrived in the first great wave of 1849 are still remembered today as the forty-niners, and their name has become part of American history.

Only a small number of the diggers grew rich, for the work was hard, the claims were crowded and the supplies were costly, and many went home with little more than they had brought. Others stayed in the new state and became farmers, shopkeepers or craftsmen, building lives that were worth more than a lucky find. The golden dream, it seems, was kinder to the careful than to the merely hopeful.

Shopkeepers who sold tools, food and clothing to the diggers often did better than the diggers themselves, for they met a need that every newcomer had. It is also worth noticing that the very first finder was not a far-travelled treasure hunter but a working carpenter who happened to be standing at the right stream. Once again, the chance had been lying close to someone who was paying attention.

Conwell's first rule is simple: do not wait for a better time or a better place, because the opportunity that matters is the one lying directly before you. People are forever promising to begin when they have more capital, more leisure or a kinder town. He replied that the best moment and the best place are, almost invariably, the present one and the nearest.

He invited his listeners to look at the people around them as though they were seeing them for the first time. What do your neighbours need, he would ask, and what would they gladly pay for if someone offered it? Those questions, he held, are the quickest road to a diamond, because the answers are usually standing next door.

It is said that before each talk Conwell took the trouble to learn about the town in which he was to speak. He asked about its shops, its factories, its schools and its leading citizens, so that he could talk about the people in front of him and not about strangers far away. Such care is probably one reason why audiences felt that he spoke to them personally.

Picture a town with a school, a mill and a railway station, the kind of place that Conwell visited again and again. Each of these has needs of its own, for the school wants books and teachers, the mill wants workers and repairs, and the station wants porters, carts and a place for travellers to eat. A person who looks at the town in this way sees a dozen small chances where others see only a quiet street.

Moving away rarely cures a restless mind, for you take yourself with you wherever you go. The lazy habit, the fear or the careless way with money that held you back at home will follow you onto the train. A mere change of place, taken by itself, solves a good deal less than most people hope that it will.

You know your own town, its customs, its seasons and its people, and that knowledge is a kind of capital that a stranger would take years to acquire. You know who is honest, who is in a hurry, who has just had a baby and who is about to open a shop. Conwell wanted his listeners to see that this ordinary knowledge was worth real money.

Your neighbours already know your name, your family and your character, and in business that counts for a great deal. Trust takes years to build, and a newcomer must start from nothing, whereas you have a head start the moment you open your door. A reputation for fairness, once earned in a small place, travels from mouth to mouth faster than any advertisement.

Starting again in a new place costs money for rent, travel and tools, and the trust of the neighbours must be earned all over again. Staying where you are saves both, and leaves your first savings free to invest in your own good idea. It is a sensible, if somewhat unglamorous, argument for staying put and making the best of the ground that you already know.

Conwell did not mean that people should sit still and wait for fortune to knock at the door. He meant that they should begin today, with the tools and the talents that they already hold, and keep going until something works. The garden, after all, only yielded its diamonds to those who were willing to stir the sand.

Here is a simple way to test the idea for yourself, and it takes only a few minutes. Write down five things that people in your street or village lack, or often complain about, and then ask which of them you could help to solve. Each of those five items is a possible beginning, and none of them requires a journey.

Conwell's rule for finding the diamond can be put in a single line: find out what people need, and then supply it. It sounds almost too simple, and yet most of the world's useful trades, from baking to banking, are built on exactly that. Whoever solves a real problem for many of his neighbours will seldom find himself short of customers.

People pay for what helps them, and not for what the maker happens to admire. A beautiful object that nobody needs will gather dust on the shelf, while a plain one that solves a pressing problem will sell out by noon. The best test of any good idea is simply whether it makes somebody's day easier to get through.

In 1854 an inventor named Elisha Otis stood on a lift platform at the New York Crystal Palace and, according to the famous story, ordered the rope to be cut, proving that his safety brake would hold. People had feared lifts because a snapped rope meant a fall, and he had solved exactly that fear. His invention helped to make tall buildings practical, and the need he met was one that everyone could understand.

Margaret Knight worked in a paper-bag factory in the 1860s, where she noticed that the bags were folded like envelopes and were awkward to fill. She designed a machine that made bags with flat bottoms, much like the grocery bags we know today, and she won a patent for it in 1871. A tiny, everyday annoyance in a busy factory had pointed her straight toward a most useful invention.

Josephine Cochrane wanted to protect her fine china from the chips and cracks that came with hand washing, and so she designed a machine to do the work with jets of soapy water. She patented it in 1886, and hotels and restaurants soon became her best customers, for they had more dishes than they could wash. She had begun by solving her own small problem and ended by solving a great many other people's.

A tailor named Jacob Davis found that the pockets of tough work trousers tore easily, so he strengthened them with small metal rivets. Lacking the money to patent the idea alone, he wrote to Levi Strauss, a merchant who supplied the cloth, and together they received a patent in 1873. The result was the blue work trousers that millions of people still wear today.

Look closely at these four inventors and the same clear pattern begins to appear in each of their stories. None of them set out to be famous or to find a treasure, but each noticed a small and real problem and then did something about it. Their diamonds were lying in the open for anyone to pick up, and they were the ones who bent down.

Three modest questions are enough to set a patient person on the road toward a personal fortune. What do the people near me find difficult, what squanders their time or their money, and what do they already pay other people to undertake? A sound answer to any one of them may prove to be the first gem in your own garden.

Not everyone has to invent a machine in order to meet a need, and Conwell would have agreed. A teacher, a cook, a tailor or a nurse serves other people every day, and each of them earns a living by being useful. Service of that kind is the oldest kind of treasure, and it is available to anyone.

Learning what people really need takes far more attention than most of us ever give. You must watch what they do, ask them kind and sensible questions, and above all listen to the answers without interrupting. The diamond hunter who listens well will often be told exactly where the treasure lies.

Begin small, says Conwell, begin where you are, and begin with what you have. The grand plan that needs a fortune, a distant city and a lucky break is usually a way of putting off the first step. A modest start made today is worth more than a magnificent start that is always planned for next year.

A good start, in Conwell's view, demands attention a great deal more than it demands cash. Many useful ideas can be tested for the price of a few materials and a few days of observation, while expensive ideas often fail precisely because nobody tested them cheaply first. Careful watching, in short, is the cheapest kind of capital that any beginner is ever likely to find.

Countless firms have begun in a kitchen, a shed or a corner of someone else's shop, with a single table, a few tools and a clear idea. Their owners had little space and little money, but they were close to their first customers and could learn from them quickly. Size and fame come later, but only if the idea at the heart of the enterprise is sound and useful.

A small start has one great advantage, which is that it lets you learn cheaply. A mistake made with a few goods and a few customers is a lesson, whereas the same mistake made with a large stock and borrowed money may be a disaster. Those who begin modestly can afford to be wrong, and being wrong is how nearly everyone learns.

Your first customers will most likely be your neighbours, and they are the best possible audience for a beginner. If they are pleased with what you offer, they will tell their friends over the garden fence, and your reputation will begin to spread without costing you a penny. If they are not pleased, they will tell you why, which is nearly as valuable.

Put aside a little money each week, even when the amount seems too small to matter, because small amounts have a way of becoming useful. A modest saving may one day buy a tool, a stock of goods or a month of study, and those things are the seeds of a trade. It is dull advice, which no one finds exciting, and yet it is advice that almost everyone would do well to follow.

Levi Strauss arrived in San Francisco in 1853 and opened a business selling cloth, clothing and other dry goods to the shops of the growing city. It was a modest beginning for a man who would later help to create one of the most famous clothing firms in the world. Great companies, as his example reminds us, are nearly always small companies that did not give up.

Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a small bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio, and they used the skills and tools of that humble trade to build gliders and then an engine-powered aeroplane. In December 1903 their machine made the first successful powered flights, on a windy beach in North Carolina. Such a world-changing idea grew from a workshop that most visitors would have thought quite ordinary.

When one small step works, the sensible thing is to take the next one, and then the one after that. Few people reach the top of a staircase in a single leap, and those who try often fall and hurt themselves. Progress that is steady, patient and a little dull is the kind that lasts.

Conwell's advice, in the end, comes down to three plain steps that any patient person can follow. First find a real need among the people near you, then plan a way to meet that need with the means that you have, and finally begin, without waiting for perfect conditions. Each step is modest, and taken together they form a road leading from an empty pocket to a useful and respected life.

Your own skills, your friends and the place where you live are your acres of diamonds, and you did not have to travel anywhere to acquire them. Each is a resource that someone has built over many years, often without noticing. The first task, then, is simply to take a careful inventory of everything that you already own.

Learning a skill and practising it until it is second nature makes you more useful to other people, and a useful person is always in demand. Employers look for those who can do something well, and customers seek out those who can solve their problems quickly. No other kind of treasure is quite as easy to carry from one place to another as a well-practised skill.

This is partly why Conwell founded his evening classes, since he saw learning as a form of digging for the treasure that lies inside every person. A clerk who learned bookkeeping, or a labourer who learned to read plans, had added a diamond to his own hands. Education, in his view, was the most reliable tool for turning daily effort into lasting value.

Benjamin Franklin was apprenticed as a boy to his older brother, a printer in Boston, and there he learned a trade that would carry him through life. He read as many books as he could borrow, and he practised writing by copying the style of good authors. The skills he built in those early years later served him as a writer, a scientist and a statesman.

A skill is built by steady practice, a little each day, in the same way that a wall is built a brick at a time. Nobody becomes truly skilled in a week, but anyone who keeps at it for a year will be astonished at how far they have come. The patience that this demands is simply the price of the diamond, and it is a price that anyone can afford to pay.

Every farmer knows that there is no shortcut to a good harvest, and that seeds must be planted, watered and weeded before anything grows. The same law governs every other kind of work, and those who hope to skip the labour usually end up with nothing to show for their hopes. Conwell's tale is a reminder that the richest ground still has to be dug.

A field at a distance always looks greener than the one beneath our feet, and the tale is a long warning against the envy that this illusion breeds. Ali Hafed pictured a faraway treasure so brightly that he overlooked the one at home. We are all tempted, now and then, to make the same mistake with our own work, our towns and our lives.

Begin by serving the people who are nearest to you, which means your family first, then your neighbours, and then the people of your town. Their needs are the easiest for you to see, and your help is the easiest for them to trust. A habit of generous service in a small circle is the best training for service in a larger one.

Friends and neighbours are part of the treasure as well, and a wise person does not neglect them while chasing something larger. They may offer advice, work, an introduction or simply the courage to try, and such gifts cannot be bought at any price. Ali Hafed, tragically, left behind the best family and the best neighbours that a man could have wished for.

A person who is truly useful has a kind of safety that money alone cannot supply, for there will always be work for someone who can do something well. Fashions change, businesses close and prices rise and fall, but a real skill, honestly practised, keeps its value through all of them. That, at bottom, is why Conwell urged ordinary people to become skilful before they tried to become rich.

Conwell took a bold position, one that some listeners found surprising from a minister: it is right, and even a duty, to become rich, so long as one does so honestly and for a good purpose. He gave this as his own opinion, and he defended it with energy in hall after hall. Whether we agree with him or not, his argument gives every thoughtful reader a good deal to think about.

Conwell believed that many kind and honest people keep away from wealth because they have been taught that wanting money is wrong. In his opinion, this belief left the world's money in the hands of the careless and the greedy, and left good people poor when they might have done a great deal of good. It was a thought-provoking argument, and it is easy to imagine that not every listener in the hall was convinced by it.

Conwell pointed out that the Bible warns against the love of money, and not against money itself, which in his view was a useful servant. A letter attributed to the apostle Paul says that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil, and the difference between loving money and using it, he argued, is the whole point. Readers from every tradition may weigh the question for themselves, and many will read the old text in their own way.

A person who is honest, who weighs fairly and keeps promises, earns a trust that no advertisement can buy. Trust brings customers back again and again, and it brings their friends along with them, so that honesty turns out to be good business as well as good conduct. Conwell never tired of making that point, which he repeated to shopkeepers, farmers and clerks in town after town.

Conwell claimed that most wealthy people had earned their money honestly, which was why people trusted them with so much. Yet in his own time, the years that we call the Gilded Age, some very large fortunes were made by bribery, fraud or the crushing of rivals, and newspapers said so loudly. Many historians would say that the truth lay somewhere between his cheerful view and his critics' harsher one.

A good name takes many years of honest work to build, and a single dishonest act can destroy it in an afternoon. For that reason a careful person guards it more jealously than any purse, since once lost it is very hard to buy back. Conwell's listeners, living in small towns where everyone knew everyone, understood this very well.

Conwell held a hard view that many readers will find unkind today, namely that most poor people were poor through their own faults. He thought that laziness, carelessness and bad habits kept them down, and he said so plainly to audiences that included people who were struggling. We should note it as his opinion, and then look at what the evidence says.

Today many economists and historians see numerous causes of poverty beyond personal fault, among them illness, accidents, low wages, lost jobs and unequal chances at school and work. A hard-working farmer may lose a crop to the weather, and a careful worker may lose a job when a factory closes. Conwell's view contains some truth, since habits matter, but it is certainly not the whole story.

Still, Conwell believed strongly in helping those who were trying to improve their lives, and he put his own money where his opinions were. Much of what he earned went to students who could not otherwise have afforded an education, and it is for this generosity that he is best remembered. A harsh opinion about the poor, it seems, can sit quite comfortably beside a very generous and helping hand.

So we may take two lessons from this part of the lecture, and hold them together. Honest effort is good, and an honest fortune is nothing to be ashamed of; yet we should be slow to judge the poor, since we rarely know the whole of another person's story. Wisdom lies, as so often, in keeping both of these thoughts firmly in view at the same time.

Money, said Conwell, is a power, and like any power it can be used well or badly. Used well, it builds schools, churches and hospitals, pays teachers and nurses, and gives help to those who would otherwise go without. He wanted his listeners to see it as a tool for good, and to feel a little less ashamed of wishing for it.

Stephen Girard, a banker and shipowner in Philadelphia, died in 1831 and left most of his large fortune to the city and to the founding of a school for poor orphan boys. Girard College opened in 1848, and it still stands in Philadelphia today, a monument to what one man's money could do. Conwell would have known it well, since he lived and worked in the same city.

Peter Cooper, a New York businessman and inventor, made a fortune from iron and from glue, and he never forgot that he had himself been short of schooling. In 1859 he opened Cooper Union, a college that offered free education to working people and that still carries his name. His example shows how a fortune earned honestly can pay for opportunities for thousands.

When Benjamin Franklin died in 1790, he left a sum of money to each of the cities of Boston and Philadelphia, with the instruction that it be lent to young craftsmen who were starting out in a trade. The fund was to grow over two centuries, and it did, paying for useful projects long after his death. Franklin had once been a poor apprentice himself, and he wanted others to have the help that he had needed.

Conwell asked those who grew rich to give wisely and not merely to keep, since he believed that wealth carries with it a duty toward other people. A gift that teaches a young person a trade may do more lasting good than a purse of coins handed over without thought, and many givers have reached that same conclusion. This was the principle that seems to have guided his own giving to the school.

You do not have to be rich in order to give, and Conwell would not have wanted anyone to believe otherwise. An hour spent teaching a child to read, a skill shared with a neighbour or a meal carried to a sick friend are gifts of real value. Some of the best help in any town is given by people who have almost no money at all.

The danger comes when money stops being a tool and becomes a master, so that a person works only for coins and forgets the people for whom the coins were meant. Conwell's warning about the love of money seems to have exactly this danger in mind. A fortune that costs a man his honesty, his health and his friends is a very poor bargain indeed.

Ali Hafed already had enough, but after the priest's visit he could no longer see it. To know what is enough is itself a kind of wealth, and it is one that a person can possess without owning a single jewel. The farmer lost it in a single evening, and he never found it again.

Wealth is not only a matter of money, and Conwell's own tale shows this very clearly. Health, a loving family, good friends, honest work and a respected name are all forms of riches, and they cannot be bought in any market. A person who has them has far more than the accounts of a bank can ever show.

At the beginning of the tale Ali Hafed possessed every one of these riches, and he gave them up for the sake of a dream that was not even his own. The priest had meant no harm, and the farmer had meant none either, which is exactly why the story is so sad. That is why the tale still stings after all these years, and why it remains well worth hearing again and again.

Greatness, says Conwell, is not a matter of fame, wealth or high office, but of doing great good wherever one happens to be. A quiet life spent serving others may therefore be greater than a loud life spent in the public eye. It was a democratic idea, and it suited the ordinary people who filled his halls.

A good teacher in a small village school may change the lives of hundreds of children over the years, and yet she will seldom be given a statue or a headline. Her pupils carry what she taught them into homes, shops and farms that she will never see. If that is not a kind of greatness, then it is very hard to say what greatness could possibly be.

Abraham Lincoln was born in 1809 in a one-room log cabin in Kentucky, and he grew up on frontier farms with very little formal schooling. He taught himself by reading whatever books he could borrow, and he became a lawyer and later the sixteenth president of the United States. His beginnings were as plain as any listener's, and that was just the point.

Conwell himself was a boy from a hill farm in a small Massachusetts town, and nothing in his early surroundings promised that he would one day address enormous crowds in great cities. His own life was a modest proof of his argument that important work can begin in the least important place. He spoke, in other words, as a living example and not as a distant expert.

Many of the people who do the greatest good come from small towns and plain homes, and are known to few outside them. The village schoolteacher, the country nurse and the careful farmer rarely appear in history books, yet their work holds a community together. A community, after all, is built far more from steady labour than from famous names.

Every famous person was once someone's neighbour, a name that few people knew and nobody expected to remember. Their first steps were taken in plain places, among ordinary tasks, long before any crowd was there to cheer them. If you are waiting for the world to notice you before you begin, you may be waiting for a very long time.

You can show real greatness in small and everyday things, and a kind act, a fair price or a promise kept at some cost to yourself is as good a place to begin as any. Such deeds rarely make the news, but they make a community worth living in. A town full of people who do them is a town full of diamonds.

A person who serves a community faithfully becomes known for it, and in time is often trusted with larger duties. The doctor who comes at night, the shopkeeper who gives fair measure and the teacher who stays late are the people to whom others turn. Conwell saw in such figures the quiet answer to his own question about where greatness might be found.

Fame is quick to fade, and the thrones that Ali Hafed once dreamed of for his sons have crumbled in the real world as surely as any kingdom of the past. A useful life, by contrast, leaves behind schools, hospitals, friendships and habits of kindness that outlast the person who began them. The tale quietly asks us which kind of legacy we would prefer to leave.

Greatness, in Conwell's sense, is open to everyone who is listening, and it need not wait for a better year or a larger stage. It can begin today, in your own street, with a single useful act done for another person. There is no entrance fee to be paid, and the door, as far as Conwell was concerned, has always stood wide open.

The lecture belongs to the time in which Conwell lived and spoke, and a modern reader should enjoy its plain wisdom while weighing its opinions and its facts with care. Some of its examples are legends rather than records, and some of its views about money and poverty have been challenged by later writers. That is no reason to put the book down, only to read it with an open and critical mind.

Times have changed, and chances were never equal for everyone, even in Conwell's own day. Women were denied the vote in national elections, many Black Americans were shut out of good schools and well-paid jobs by law and custom, and newcomers from other lands were often treated with suspicion. For people in those positions, some barriers could not be dug away by hard work alone.

Where the barriers are real, the lesson becomes a double one: look for what you can use close to you, and also work with others to change what is unfair. In Conwell's century and since, people have built schools, formed unions, won the vote and opened doors that were once shut, and each of those victories created new acres for those who came after. A garden can be improved and made fairer for everyone, as well as simply dug.

The whole lecture can be boiled down to four ideas that fit easily into a notebook. Find a real need near you, serve it honestly, build a skill that makes you useful, and keep working steadily even when progress seems slow. None of the four requires a fortune, a miracle or a long journey, only a clear head and a willingness to begin.

Conwell hoped that those who succeeded by this road would remember what money is for, and would spend it on schools, hospitals and the happiness of others. He hoped, too, that they would find contentment in a useful life, and not merely in a growing pile of coins. In that hope, the end of the lecture comes back to the contented man at the beginning of the tale.

Ali Hafed is not a villain, and nobody in the tale is one, for the priest meant well and the new owner simply picked up what lay at his feet. Ali Hafed was a good man with a restless wish, and his story is sad because it could have ended so differently. That is the secret of its power, for each listener is able to find a little of himself in it.

The tale of Ali Hafed has been retold in many books, sermons and speeches, and plenty of people who have never read the lecture know the story of the farmer, the priest and the camel. Each teller changes the details a little, as the guide himself may once have done, but the heart of the tale survives every retelling. It is the mark of a good story that it can travel so far and still be recognised.

When you close the book, try looking at your own street as though you were a stranger seeing it for the first time. The shop that is always empty, the school that needs helpers and the neighbour who cannot find a tradesman are all clues that something is waiting to be done. In that new light, a familiar place may begin to look quite different from the one that you thought you knew so well.

Before you go, take a sheet of paper and set down three lists: the abilities you possess, the acquaintances you value and the needs that you can observe nearby. Then draw a line from each ability to a need that it might meet, and from each friend to the help that they might offer. Within a few minutes you may discover that your acres of diamonds already have a rough map.

Conwell ended his lecture with a question that every listener could take home, and the question is still open: where are your own acres of diamonds? They may lie in a skill you have not yet used, in a neighbour whose need you have not yet noticed, or in the work that lies at your own door. Dig there first, he would say, before you set out to look anywhere else.
